paragraphs: # What it is

Wrestling is fighting with your bare hands. It is also what protects you when your hands are empty: the skill of the weapon you hold is the skill used to dodge blows, so a swordsman is defended by Swordsmanship and someone holding nothing is defended by Wrestling. Monsters that carry no weapon defend with their Wrestling skill, so that is the number you have to beat in those fights.
# How it works

Take your weapon off and attack. Fists do 1 to 8 damage and have a speed of 30. After every swing you wait 15000 divided by ((your stamina + 100) times the weapon's speed) seconds: 75 divided by the speed at 100 stamina. Your stamina can never be higher than your Dexterity, so a low Dexterity means slow swings. For fists that is 2.5 seconds at 100 stamina. For comparison, a Katana does 5 to 26 and swings every 1.3 seconds.

Your chance to hit is (your skill + 50) divided by twice (their skill + 50): equal skills hit half the time, skill 100 against 50 three times in four, skill 50 against 100 one time in three. Once your skill reaches twice theirs plus 50 you hit every time, and a swing that cannot miss teaches you nothing.

Damage is the weapon's range changed by your Tactics (half at Tactics 0, unchanged at 50, one and a half times at 100), plus 1% for every 5 points of Strength and 1% for every 5 points of Anatomy. Armor and tough hides take points off, a hit never does less than 1, and against another player damage is halved.

Wrestling could once Stun and Disarm. Those moves are switched off on this shard: if your client shows buttons for them they do nothing, and the server says so. No weapon has an automatic special blow here either.
# Training it
Take off any weapon first, or the swings train that weapon instead. Training only works while the skill is set to Up in your skills window (see Skill locks 101 in [Welcome).

From 0 to 25: stand next to a training dummy in Britain with empty hands and double-click it. A dummy allows one practice swing about every 3 seconds, not from a mount, and it refuses once the skill reaches 25.0.

After the dummy, fight creatures. A monster that carries no weapon defends with its own Wrestling skill: the harder it is to hit, the more a swing can teach, and you stop learning from it once your skill reaches about twice its Wrestling plus 50. Wrestling skill and hit points of some monsters:
Rat: 4; 6 hit points. It stops teaching at about 60.
Headless One: 25 to 40; 16 to 30 hit points
Zombie: 35 to 50; 28 to 42
Skeleton: 45 to 55; 34 to 48
Orc, Lizardman and Ratman: 50 to 75; 58 to 72
Ettin: 50 to 60; 82 to 99
Troll: 50 to 70; 106 to 123
Ogre: 70 to 80; 100 to 117
None of the others stops teaching before 100.
Snakes, giant spiders, scorpions, wraiths and spectres can poison you: see the Healing page for curing.
The Mage Guildmaster in Britain teaches Wrestling for gold, up to a third of its own skill (about 20 to 28). See Training in [Welcome.

paragraphs: # What it is

Archery is the skill of bows and crossbows. You shoot from up to 10 tiles away with a bow, or 8 with a crossbow, and every shot uses up an arrow or a bolt. While you hold a ranged weapon you hit with Archery and you are defended by it.
# How it works

A bow takes arrows and a crossbow takes bolts, one for every shot, from your pack. You must see your target, and you must stand still to shoot: after you move you cannot shoot until you have been still for 1 second at Dexterity 25 or less, down to half a second at Dexterity 100 (about 0.95 seconds at Dexterity 33). Moving starts the wait again.

After every swing you wait 15000 divided by ((your stamina + 100) times the weapon's speed) seconds: 75 divided by the speed at 100 stamina. Your stamina can never be higher than your Dexterity, so a low Dexterity means slow swings. That is 3.75 seconds for a Bow, 4.2 for a Crossbow and 7.5 for a Heavy Crossbow at 100 stamina.
A bow and both crossbows are two-handed, so you cannot hold a shield. A heavier weapon needs more Strength, and you cannot equip a weapon if your Strength is below what it needs.

Your chance to hit is (your skill + 50) divided by twice (their skill + 50): equal skills hit half the time, skill 100 against 50 three times in four, skill 50 against 100 one time in three. Once your skill reaches twice theirs plus 50 you hit every time, and a swing that cannot miss teaches you nothing.

Damage is the weapon's range changed by your Tactics (half at Tactics 0, unchanged at 50, one and a half times at 100), plus 1% for every 5 points of Strength and 1% for every 5 points of Anatomy. Armor and tough hides take points off, a hit never does less than 1, and against another player damage is halved. An archer with Strength 54, Anatomy 0 and Tactics 50 hits for about 28 with a Bow.

A shot that misses leaves its arrow on the ground near the target 4 times in 10, and a shot that hits a monster or animal puts the arrow in its pack 4 times in 10: look in the corpse. Other ammunition is gone.
# Training it
Training only works while the skill is set to Up in your skills window (see Skill locks 101 in [Welcome).

Stand in front of the butte in a straight line, 5 or 6 tiles away (closer or farther and it complains), and double-click it to shoot. Double-click it from next to it to gather your arrows. You can shoot once every 2 seconds, each shot uses a piece of ammunition, and it stops teaching when your skill reaches about 25.

paragraphs: # What it is

Parrying is the skill of fighting with a shield. A shield does nothing for your chance to be hit. It works after you have been hit, when it may block part of the blow, and Parrying decides how well it does that.
# How it works
A shield goes in your off hand, so it needs a one-handed weapon, or empty hands: bows, staves, spears, axes and every other two-handed weapon use the same slot and cannot be held with a shield.

Each time a weapon hit lands on you, your shield gets one roll. The chance that it blocks is (your Parrying - 2 times the shield's armor rating) divided by 100, and never less than 1 in 100. A block takes off half the shield's armor rating (rounded down) from the hit, or the whole rating against an arrow or a bolt, though a hit still does at least 1. Parrying does nothing against spells or poison.

A shield's armor rating is its base rating times your Parrying divided by 200, plus 1, so shields get better as you train. At Parrying 50 and at 100, for an undamaged shield, the chance to block and the damage a block removes from a sword blow (an arrow loses about twice as much):
Buckler (base 7): 45% and 1, then 91% and 2
Wooden Shield (8): 44% and 1, then 90% and 2
Metal Kite Shield (16): 40% and 2, then 82% and 4
Heater Shield (23): 37% and 3, then 75% and 6
Small shields block more often and big ones block more, though even a Heater Shield removes only a few points from a blow.

Parrying does not lower your chance of being hit: that depends on your weapon skill, or on Wrestling with empty hands. A shield is worn down by blocking (about 1 block in 8 costs it a point of durability), and a damaged shield has a lower rating.
# Training it
Training only works while the skill is set to Up in your skills window (see Skill locks 101 in [Welcome).

Parrying is checked each time a weapon hits you while you carry a shield, whether the shield blocks or not, and the check does not depend on who hits you. A training dummy does not train it. A rat's bite, for example, does only 1 point. It never stops teaching before 100, because the chance to block is never certain.
The Blacksmith and the Warrior Guildmaster in Britain teach Parrying for gold, up to a third of their own skill (about 20 to 33). See Training in [Welcome.

paragraphs: # What it is
Tactics is the skill of fighting well. You never use it: it works on its own whenever you land a blow, and it changes how hard that blow hits.
# How it works

Your Tactics scales every hit you land: damage is cut by half at Tactics 0, is unchanged at 50 and is one and a half times as large at 100. Each point is 1%, so at 25 you do 25% less and at 75 you do 25% more. It does not change your chance to hit, your swing speed or how hard monsters hit you, and it works with every weapon, fists and bows included. Monsters have Tactics too, and it shapes their blows the same way.
None of the ready-made starting templates includes Tactics, so a new fighter usually begins at 0, where every hit does half damage.

Strength and Anatomy then add to the result, 1% for every 5 points of each. A Grandmaster with Strength 100 and Anatomy 100 therefore does 2.1 times the weapon's damage. A fighter with Tactics 0, Strength 54 and Anatomy 35 does about 0.6 times. Against another player the damage is halved after all of that.
# Training it
Training only works while the skill is set to Up in your skills window (see Skill locks 101 in [Welcome).

There is no button. Tactics is checked each time you land a hit on something, and nothing else trains it: not misses, not being hit, not spells. The check does not depend on your chance to hit, so it keeps teaching even against creatures that are too easy to teach your weapon skill. A fast weapon lands more hits and so trains it faster. It does not stop before 100.

So any fight in which you land blows trains it. The Blacksmith, the Warrior Guildmaster and the Rangers' Guildmaster in Britain teach Tactics for gold, up to a third of their own skill (about 20 to 33). See Training in [Welcome.

Nothing. Any weapon will do, and every hit you land counts.
# Good to know
Tactics and Anatomy do not make you harder to hit or let you hit more often. They only make each hit hurt more.
# What it is

Anatomy is knowing how bodies work. It makes every blow you land hit harder and every bandage you apply heal more, and it lets you look a creature or person over to see how strong and nimble they are.
# How it works

Every 5 points of Anatomy add 1% to every hit you land, so 20% at 100, on any weapon. A Grandmaster gets nothing extra on top of that here. Each 5 points also add 1 to both the least and the most that a bandage heals. A bandage can cure poison only if both your Healing and your Anatomy are at least 60, and bring someone back from the dead only if both are at least 80: see the Healing page.

To look someone over, click the button beside Anatomy in your skills window and then click a creature or person within 8 tiles. You are told how strong and how nimble they look, and with Anatomy 65 or more also how much stamina they have left, in tens of percent. The lower your skill the less exact the answer, which can be off by up to 25 points at skill 0 and is exact at 100. You cannot look at yourself, and invulnerable town vendors cannot be looked over. You can use another skill 1 second later.
# Training it
Training only works while the skill is set to Up in your skills window (see Skill locks 101 in [Welcome).

Use the skill on a living target, again and again. Each use is a skill check with a chance of skill divided by 100, so you fail often at first, and a failed use still counts toward your training. It costs nothing and risks nothing if the target is peaceful: your own pet, a friend, or a rat, cat, dog or bird in Britain's streets. It stops teaching at 100.
Anatomy also trains from fighting: it is checked every time you land a hit, and when a bandage finishes on a wounded patient. Both ways teach it right up to 100.
The Healer Guildmaster in Britain and wandering healers in the countryside teach Anatomy for gold, up to a third of their own skill (about 25 to 33). See Training in [Welcome.

paragraphs.text: Faint Memories: a new character's free points come back as you train a skill set to Up, 0.2 at a time, between 10.0 and 80.0, starting 24 hours after the character was created. [SkillBank shows what is left.

paragraphs: # What you need
Nothing. Anatomy works best with Tactics and Healing: all three raise your damage or your healing, and a bandage trains Anatomy and Healing together.
# Good to know
Anatomy does not change how often you hit or are hit. It changes how hard you hit and how much you heal.
For healing, Anatomy is worth a flat bonus: at Healing 100 a bandage heals 23 to 60 hit points with Anatomy 0 and 43 to 80 with Anatomy 100.
# What it is

Healing is the skill of bandages. A bandage heals wounds and cures poison, and at high skill it can bring a dead player back to life. Anatomy works beside it: the two skills are trained together and add together.
# How to use it

Double-click bandages in your pack and then click who to bandage: yourself, or someone standing next to you. The patient must be within 1 tile when you start, and you must still be within 1 tile when you finish, or the bandage is wasted. Nothing happens at once: it takes effect when the wait ends.

On yourself the wait is 9.4 seconds plus 0.6 seconds for every 10 points your Dexterity is below 120 (14.6 seconds at Dexterity 33, 10.6 at 100). On someone else it is 5 seconds at Dexterity under 40, 4 seconds from 40 and 3 seconds from 100, plus 5 more seconds if the patient is dead.

What a finished bandage does depends on the patient. (In these numbers Healing is the value the Stats section below describes; Anatomy counts exactly as shown.) A wounded patient is healed only if a roll succeeds, with a chance of (Healing + 10) in 100. It then heals between (Anatomy / 5 + Healing / 5 + 3) and (Anatomy / 5 + Healing / 2 + 10) hit points. At Healing 0 and Anatomy 0 that is a 1 in 10 chance for 3 to 10 points, at 50 and 50 it is 60% for 23 to 45, and at 100 and 100 it always works for 43 to 80.
Any damage you take while bandaging makes your fingers slip, poison included: each slip lowers the chance by 2 points in 100 and the healing by 4 hit points. Fight first, then bandage.

Poison: a bandage on a poisoned patient only tries to cure, and only if your Healing and Anatomy are both at least 60. The chance is (Healing - 30) in 50, minus 10 in 100 for each step of the poison (Lesser 0, Regular 1, Greater 2, Deadly 3, Lethal 4). At Healing 80 a Lesser poison is always cured and at 100 any poison is. If either skill is under 60 the bandage cannot work and is used up all the same. A poisoned patient is not healed: cure first.

Resurrection: a bandage on a dead player standing next to you tries to bring them back, only if your Healing and Anatomy are both at least 80. The chance is (Healing - 68) in 50: 24% at 80, 44% at 90, 64% at 100. On success the player is offered a window to accept. Coming back costs no skill or stats on this shard.
# Training it
Training only works while the skill is set to Up in your skills window (see Skill locks 101 in [Welcome).

Healing and Anatomy both train each time a bandage finishes on a wounded patient, whether it heals or fails. Curing and resurrecting train them only when the attempt works, which needs the skill minimum. Healing's check is your skill out of 120, so it keeps teaching right up to 100.
So the way up is to bandage something wounded, again and again: yourself, or a friend. A bandage on a tamed animal uses Veterinary instead of Healing, so train Healing on people.
The Healer and the Healer Guildmaster in Britain and wandering healers in the countryside teach Healing for gold, up to a third of their own skill (about 25 to 33). See Training in [Welcome.

paragraphs.text: Poison relief: a character created while it is on starts with 5 Lesser Cure potions (an alchemist sells them for about 15 gold). The first time you are poisoned while your Healing or Anatomy is under 60, you are told why a bandage will not help. For 30 seconds after a poison ends, Lesser poison from a monster or trap cannot land on you again.

Faint Memories: a new character's free points come back as you train a skill set to Up, 0.2 at a time, between 10.0 and 80.0, starting 24 hours after the character was created. [SkillBank shows what is left.

paragraphs: # What you need

Bandages. The Healer in Britain sells them for about 5 gold each and keeps 20 in stock. You can also cut cloth into bandages with scissors, one bandage for each cloth: tailors in Britain sell cloth for about 2 gold, scissors for about 11, and a bolt of cloth for about 100 gold that cuts into 50 cloth.

paragraphs.text: Anyone who starts with Swordsmanship, Mace Fighting, Fencing or Archery begins with 50 bandages.

paragraphs: # Good to know
Do not start a second bandage while one is working. It cancels the first, which is already used up.
A bandage on someone at full health who is not poisoned is refused and not used. If they reach full health before the wait ends, the bandage does nothing more and trains nothing.
Bandaging a criminal or a murderer is a criminal act and makes you a criminal too.

paragraphs.text: Helping a player who only has Criminal Intent switched on (see Fighting other players in [Welcome) does not make you a criminal.
A Knocked Out player cannot be bandaged, and cannot bandage.

paragraphs: A heal potion will not help a poisoned person either: cure the poison first.
# What it is

Magery is the skill of casting spells: 64 of them, in eight circles. The higher the circle, the more mana a spell costs and the more skill it needs. Mana is the magic a spell spends, and the most you can hold is your Intelligence. Cast from a book, every spell also burns reagents, small ingredients you carry: Black Pearl, Bloodmoss, Garlic, Ginseng, Mandrake Root, Nightshade, Sulfurous Ash and Spider's Silk.

A mage also wants Evaluating Intelligence (harder hits), Meditation (mana back sooner) and Resisting Spells (less harm from other casters). The four take 400 of the 700 skill points a character can hold.
# Casting a spell

Double-click your Spellbook to open it, then double-click a spell; or double-click a spell scroll in your backpack. The book must hold the spell and be in your hand or lie directly in your backpack, not inside a bag. Most spells then ask for a target within 10 tiles and in sight (Night Sight 12, field spells 15, Resurrection 1). You have 30 seconds to choose.

You stand still while casting: 0.5 seconds for a first-circle spell, 0.25 more for each circle, 2.25 for the eighth (Blade Spirits and Summon Creature take four times as long). The next spell can start 0.75 seconds after the cast time ends. Casting puts any weapon or shield in your hands into your backpack (the spellbook stays) and reveals you if you were hidden.

A spell takes mana only if it works: 4, 6, 9, 11, 14, 20, 40 and 50 for circles one to eight. From a book it also burns one of each reagent it lists, taken from your backpack or any bag in it. From a scroll it uses up the scroll and no reagents, and its skill range starts 20 points lower (40 lower in the second circle, 50 lower in the first). To keep a scroll's spell in your book, click the scroll once, choose Add To Spellbook and click the book.
# When a spell fails

Each cast is a skill check against the range listed with each circle. Below its first number the spell always fizzles ('The spell fizzles.'); from there the chance rises evenly to certain at the second number. A fizzle costs the reagents but not the mana, and a scroll is not used up. You learn only from checks between the two numbers.

Damage ruins a spell while it is being cast (poison too), and so does putting something on. First-circle spells cannot be broken by damage. A ruined spell costs nothing, but you cannot cast for 0.2 to 1 second (longer the sooner you were hit). Double-clicking an item or a creature while the target cursor is up cancels the spell, also at no cost. Protection (second circle) gives you a chance to shrug off a hit.
# What your skills change

The base damage of Magic Arrow, Harm, Fireball, Lightning, Mind Blast, Energy Bolt, Explosion, Flamestrike, Chain Lightning and Meteor Swarm (in the lists below) is cut if the target resists, then multiplied by 1 + (your Evaluating Intelligence - the target's Resisting Spells) / 500, divided by 200 instead when that difference is below zero, + (your Magery - 100) / 400. With 100.0 in both against a target with none that is x1.2. Against anything without a human body (animals, undead, dragons, orcs; not players or person-shaped creatures) it is doubled. Armor does not reduce spell damage. The Evaluating Intelligence and Resisting Spells pages say more.

A stat spell (Clumsy, Feeblemind, Weaken, Agility, Cunning, Strength, Bless, Curse, Mass Curse) changes a stat by 1 + Magery / 10 (rounded down) for 1.2 seconds per Magery point: 11 points for 2 minutes at 100.0. The curses are never resisted.
# Training it

A Pure Mage starts with 50.0 Magery, a Warlock with 48.0 and a Sorcerer with 36.0. A mage in Britain also teaches it for 1 gold per 0.1 point, up to a third of its own skill: about 21 to 33 (see Training in the Welcome guide, [Welcome).

To train, cast. A cast teaches only while your skill is between the two numbers of its range, so move up a circle as you improve: cast the circle equal to your skill divided by ten, rounded down (a first-circle spell until 20.0). From 10.0, each cast then works one time in four or better. These need no victim; the costs are mana and reagents at vendor prices:
Up to 19: Night Sight on yourself. 4 mana, 6 gold.
20 to 29: Strength on yourself. 6 mana, 6 gold.
30 to 39: Bless on yourself. 9 mana, 6 gold.
40 to 49: Arch Cure on yourself. 11 mana, 9 gold.
50 to 59: Poison Field on open ground, outside town. 14 mana, 11 gold.
60 to 69: Reveal on open ground. 20 mana, 8 gold.
70 and up: Mass Dispel on open ground. 40 mana, 14 gold.

A spell with a victim can cost less (Magic Arrow 3 gold, Flamestrike 6 gold). Mana is the limit, not gold: cast until nearly empty, then use Meditation or wait. Every cast also trains Evaluating Intelligence. A spell stops teaching at the second number of its range: 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90, 100 and 110 for circles one to eight. From 80.0 Mastery's daily sure gains are paid for by successful casts that could have failed, so keep to a circle whose second number is above your skill.
# What you need

A Mage in Britain sells the Spellbook (18 gold), scrolls of the first three circles only (12, 22 and 32 gold each), Recall Runes (15 gold) and reagents (3 gold each, 5 for Black Pearl and Bloodmoss). Alchemists sell the same reagents. Scrolls of the higher circles turn up as loot or are made by players with Inscription. Reagents also lie in the wild.

A character who starts with Magery begins with a Spellbook holding 12 spells (Heal, Magic Arrow, Night Sight, Cure, Harm, Strength, Fireball, Poison, Teleport, Fire Field, Greater Heal and Lightning), three scrolls and a Bag of Reagents. The Spellbook is blessed: you keep it when you die.

paragraphs.text: The Bag of Reagents holds 50 of each of the eight reagents.

paragraphs: # Good to know

Reagents are spent before the skill check, so a fizzle costs them; an area spell burns them even if nothing is in reach.
Armor never slows casting, but anything heavier than leather slows how fast your mana comes back (see Meditation).
Reactive Armor, Protection and Magic Reflection share one slot: while one is in force, and for a minute after it ends or is used up, another is refused ('The spell will not adhere to you at this time.').
Heal and Greater Heal do nothing for a poisoned target: cure the poison first.
Helping a criminal or a murderer with a spell makes you a criminal too.
# The spells

Reagents are written BP Black Pearl, BM Bloodmoss, GA Garlic, GI Ginseng, MR Mandrake Root, NS Nightshade, SA Sulfurous Ash, SS Spider's Silk; a spell burns one of each it lists. A spell takes one creature or player as its target unless the line says otherwise: 'ground' is a spot you click, 'self' is you alone. 'N followers' is how many of your 5 follower slots a summon takes. 'Not in town' marks a spell you cannot cast in a guarded town ('You cannot cast this in town!'). Each circle gives the mana, then the skill range for a book and for a scroll.
# First circle

4 mana. Book 0 to 40, scroll -50 to -10.
Clumsy (BM NS): Dexterity down.
Create Food (GA GI MR): no target; a random food in your backpack.
Feeblemind (GI NS): Intelligence down.
Heal (GA GI SS): heals Magery / 10 + 1 to 5.
Magic Arrow (SA): 4 to 7 damage.
Night Sight (SA SS): light in the dark for a random 15 to 39 minutes, as long as a Night Sight potion lasts; the light is stronger with more Magery (none at 0).
Reactive Armor (GA SS SA): self; absorbs blows from weapons (arrows too), in all (Magery + Meditation + Inscription) / 3 points (75 at most), though each absorbed blow still does 1, and hits back for a fifth of each blow (at least 1); a blow bigger than what is left goes through and ends it. No time limit.
Weaken (GA NS): Strength down.
# Second circle

6 mana. Book 10 to 50, scroll -30 to 10.
Agility (BM MR): Dexterity up.
Cunning (MR NS): Intelligence up.
Cure (GA GI): tries to cure poison. At Magery 100.0 it always works except on Lethal poison (87 in 100); at 50.0 it fails 15 times in 100 on Greater poison.
Harm (NS SS): 1 to 15 damage.
Magic Trap (GA SS SA): a chest or box; the first person to open it from next to it takes 1 damage.
Magic Untrap (BM SA): a chest or box; removes a magic trap, fizzles on any other trap.
Protection (GA GI SA): self; for twice your Magery in seconds (200 at 100.0, 15 at least) each hit has a chance, (Evaluating Intelligence + Meditation + Inscription) / 4 percent (75 at most), of not ruining your cast.
Strength (MR NS): Strength up.
# Third circle

9 mana. Book 20 to 60, scroll 0 to 40.
Bless (GA MR): Strength, Dexterity and Intelligence up.
Fireball (BP): 10 to 16 damage.
Magic Lock (GA BM SA): an unlocked chest or box; it cannot be picked, and only its key or Unlock opens it.
Poison (NS): poisons unless resisted. Magery + Poisoning set the strength: Lesser up to 130.2, Regular over 130.2, Greater over 170.2, and over 199.8 Greater or, one time in ten, Deadly. The sum drops by 10 for each tile beyond 3.
Telekinesis (BM MR): a door, container or dice; you use it from afar, and a trap on it cannot reach you beyond 3 tiles.
Teleport (BM MR): ground; you appear there. Not into a house or boat, and not while overloaded.
Unlock (BM SA): a locked chest or box; it opens if 0.8 x Magery - 4 reaches its lock.
Wall of Stone (BM GA): ground within 15; three stones of wall for 10 seconds. Not in town.
# Fourth circle

11 mana. Book 30 to 70, scroll 10 to 50.
Arch Cure (GA GI MR): ground or creature; tries to cure everyone within 2 tiles, friend or foe, about as surely as Cure, except against Lethal poison.
Arch Protection (GA GI MR SA): ground or creature; everyone within 3 tiles gets Magery / 10 + 1 extra armor rating for 1.2 seconds per Magery point (2 minutes at 100.0), unless they already have it.
Curse (NS GA SA): Strength, Dexterity and Intelligence down.
Fire Field (BP SS SA): ground within 15; five fire tiles for as many seconds as your Magery; 2 damage a second (1 if the victim passes a Resisting Spells check up to 30). Not in town.
Greater Heal (GA GI MR SS): heals 0.4 x Magery + 1 to 10.
Lightning (MR SA): 12 to 20 damage.
Mana Drain (BP MR SS): resisted 99 times in 100; otherwise drains 1 to 100 mana (what it has).
Recall (BP BM MR): a marked rune; carries you to it.
# Fifth circle

14 mana. Book 40 to 80, scroll 20 to 60.
Blade Spirits (BP MR NS): ground; Blade Spirits fight for you for 80 to 119 seconds. 1 follower. Cast time 6 seconds. Not in town.
Dispel Field (BP SS SA GA): a field spell or Gate Travel gate within 15; removes it.
Incognito (BM GA NS): self; a new name, skin and hair for 1.2 seconds per Magery point (2 minutes at 100.0).
Magic Reflection (GA MR SS): self; single-target harmful spells cast at you go back to their caster until 8 to 15 circles' worth have been reflected (Magery + Inscription; a spell counts as its circle number). No time limit.
Mind Blast (BP MR NS SA): half the gap between the target's highest and lowest stat, 45 at most.
Paralyze (GA MR SS): frozen for 7 seconds + Magery / 5; any damage frees it.
Poison Field (BP NS SS): ground within 15; five tiles for 15 seconds + 0.4 per Magery point; whoever steps in is poisoned (Regular). Not in town.
Summon Creature (BM MR SS): self; a random creature (a bear, wolf, horse and the like) fights for you for 4 seconds per Magery point. Needs 2 free follower slots to cast; the creature takes 1. Cast time 6 seconds. Not in town.
# Sixth circle

20 mana. Book 50 to 90, scroll 30 to 70.
Dispel (GA MR SA): a summoned creature; destroyed with a chance of 50 percent + 2.5 per Magery point above its difficulty (Blade Spirits 0, Energy Vortex 80, elementals 117.5, daemon 125).
Energy Bolt (BP NS): 24 to 41 damage.
Explosion (BM MR): 23 to 44 damage, 2.5 seconds after the cast.
Invisibility (BM NS): hides the target (not a shopkeeper) for 1.2 seconds per Magery point.
Mark (BP BM MR): a Recall Rune in your backpack; saves the spot where you stand.
Mass Curse (GA NS MR SA): ground; Strength, Dexterity and Intelligence down for creatures within 2 tiles of the spot. Not in town.
Paralyze Field (BP GI SS): ground within 15; five tiles for 15 seconds + Magery / 3; whoever steps in is frozen for 7 seconds + Magery / 5. Not in town.
Reveal (BM SA): ground; shows every hidden creature within 1 + Magery / 20 tiles.
# Seventh circle

40 mana. Book 60 to 100, scroll 40 to 80.
Chain Lightning (BP BM MR SA): ground; 27 to 48 damage to everyone within 2 tiles, split among them if there are more than two; you too if you stand there. Not in town.
Energy Field (BP MR SS SA): ground within 15; a five-tile wall for 2 seconds + 0.28 per Magery point. Not in town.
Flamestrike (SS SA): 27 to 48 damage (three fifths if resisted).
Gate Travel (BP MR SA): a marked rune; opens a gate where you stand and one at the rune, both for 30 seconds.
Mana Vampire (BP BM MR SS): resisted 98 times in 100; otherwise all the target's mana is taken and you gain as much of it as you can hold.
Mass Dispel (GA MR BP SA): ground; Dispel on every summoned creature within 8 tiles.
Meteor Swarm (BM MR SA SS): ground; 27 to 48 damage split among everyone within 2 tiles, not you. Not in town.
Polymorph (BM SS MR): self; you choose one of 18 shapes for 120 seconds.
# Eighth circle

50 mana. Book 70 to 110, scroll 50 to 90.
Earthquake (BM GI MR SA): around you; everything within 1 + Magery / 15 tiles loses 60 percent of its hit points (a monster at least 10, none more than 75), not you. Not in town.
Energy Vortex (BM BP MR NS): ground; an Energy Vortex fights for you for 90 seconds. 1 follower. Not in town.
Resurrection (BM GA GI): a dead player next to you; offers them life. Not yourself.
Air Elemental (BM MR SS): self; 2 followers.
Earth Elemental (BM MR SS): self; 2 followers.
Water Elemental (BM MR SS): self; 3 followers.
Fire Elemental (BM MR SS SA): self; 4 followers.
Summon Daemon (BM MR SS SA): self; 5 followers, and 70 karma (reputation) lost.
The elementals and the daemon last 4 seconds per Magery point (at least 20) and are not for use in town.
# Fields and summons

A field spell lays a line of 3 or 5 tiles across the spot you pick. It appears a moment after the cast and fades by itself; Dispel Field removes it. A harmful field, Chain Lightning, Meteor Swarm and Earthquake skip your party, your guild and its allies, your pets and any player who shows as innocent (blue), and a field hurts you if you walk into it.

A summon is a follower, and you have 5 follower slots, shared with your tamed pets; with too few free the spell is refused ('You have too many followers to summon that creature.'). The elementals, the daemon and the creature from Summon Creature follow you and obey pet orders. Blade Spirits and the Energy Vortex fight on their own. A summon ends when its time runs out or it dies; Dispel destroys it.

paragraphs.text: A tamed pet cannot stay in a dungeon, but your spell summons can.

paragraphs: # Recall and Gate Travel

A Recall Rune holds a place. Stand where you want it, cast Mark and click the rune (it must be in your backpack); double-click a marked rune to name it. Cast Recall and click the rune to be there at once. Gate Travel opens two gates instead, one where you stand and one at the rune, for 30 seconds, and anyone can step through.

Neither works while you are a criminal or within 30 seconds of attacking a player, and Recall also fails when you are overloaded. Recall, Gate Travel and Mark do not work into or out of a dungeon, Khaldun or the Lost Lands. A rune cannot be marked inside a house, and Recall or a gate will not take you to a spot inside one. The destination must be open ground. You leave a dungeon on foot.

paragraphs.text: A player who is not a criminal or a murderer is asked to confirm before Recall or a gate takes them into a Hot Zone from outside one. The window has a box to stop the question, and [TravelWarning on brings it back.

paragraphs: # Safe World and Hot Zones

paragraphs.text: A harmful spell can be cast at another player only if that player has Criminal Intent on ([Intent), is a criminal or a murderer, is already fighting you, or is at guild war with you (see Fighting other players in the Welcome guide, [Welcome). Anything else is refused ('You cannot perform negative acts on your target.') before it costs you mana or reagents. Helping spells have no such limit.
In a Hot Zone, a place where players may fight freely (Fire Island, Buccaneer's Den island and Hythloth), you can aim a spell at any player in the same Hot Zone as you, with or without Intent.
A Knocked Out player cannot be harmed, healed or cured by spells. If you are Knocked Out your mana falls to 0 and a spell you were casting is lost; you wake with half your mana.

paragraphs: # What it is
Evaluating Intelligence, or Eval Int, makes your damage spells hit harder. It is also a skill you can use to size up a creature or a player.
# What it adds

The damage of Magic Arrow, Harm, Fireball, Lightning, Mind Blast, Energy Bolt, Explosion, Flamestrike, Chain Lightning and Meteor Swarm is multiplied by 1 + (your Evaluating Intelligence - the target's Resisting Spells) / 500, divided by 200 instead when your skill is the lower. So each point above the target's Resisting Spells adds 0.2 percent, and each point below takes away 0.5 percent. With your Magery at 100.0, so that its own part of the multiplier is neutral:
Evaluating Intelligence 100.0 against Resisting Spells 0.0: 20 percent more damage
100.0 against 50.0: 10 percent more
100.0 against 100.0: no change
50.0 against 100.0: 25 percent less
0.0 against 100.0: 50 percent less

Your Magery is in the same multiplier (25 percent less at Magery 0.0, nothing at 100.0), and a spell that hits a creature without a human body does double on top. Evaluating Intelligence does not change your mana, how long a spell lasts or how much Heal heals; those follow Intelligence and Magery. It does help Protection: that spell's chance to keep a hit from ruining a cast is a quarter of Evaluating Intelligence + Meditation + Inscription.
# Sizing someone up

Open your skills window and click the small button beside Evaluating Intelligence, then click a creature or a player within 8 tiles. You are told how intelligent it looks. The reading is rough: it can be off by 20 points of Intelligence, less a fifth of your skill (so it is exact at 100.0). From 76.0 you are also told how full its mana is, in steps of ten percent, with the same error in percent. A failed check says you cannot judge. It does not work on yourself, on a shopkeeper or on an object, and you must wait a second between uses.
# Training it

A mage trains it without trying. Every spell you finish casting, with its reagents and mana in hand, rolls Evaluating Intelligence as well as Magery, whether the spell works or fizzles. A spell ruined by a hit, or one you could not pay for, does not.

The skill also trains by use: the chance to read a target right is your skill out of 120. It costs nothing, and any living creature will do, such as an animal, a bystander or a monster you keep at a safe distance. A Pure Mage starts with 35.0. A mage, a scribe or the mage guildmaster in Britain teaches it for 1 gold per 0.1 point, up to a third of its own skill: about 20 to 33 (see Training in the Welcome guide, [Welcome).
# What you need
Nothing: no tool, no reagent.
# Good to know

The target's Resisting Spells is set against your skill. A mage with 100.0 Evaluating Intelligence and 100.0 Magery does 20 percent more than a spell's base damage to a target with none, but no more than the base to one with 100.0.
It stops teaching at 100.0.
# What it is
Meditation brings your mana back faster. It works on its own all the time, and you can also use it to enter a trance that doubles the speed.
# How fast mana comes back

You regain mana one point at a time. The wait for each point falls as your Intelligence plus your Meditation, halved, rises: 7 seconds at 0, 3 seconds at 50, 1 second at 100. For example:
Intelligence 40, Meditation 0.0: 5.2 seconds a point
40 and 50.0: 3.3 seconds
60 and 60.0: 2.5 seconds
100 and 100.0: 1.0 second
In a trance each wait is halved, though never to less than half a second. Intelligence counts as much as Meditation, so raise both.
# Going into a trance

Open your skills window and click the small button beside Meditation. Your hands must be free: a spellbook or runebook may stay in hand, a weapon or shield may not ('Your hands must be free to cast spells or meditate.'). You need at least a tenth of your hit points, a mana that is not full, and no target cursor open.

Your chance is 50 percent plus 2 for every point of Meditation, minus 2 for every point of mana you are missing. At 0.0 you can succeed only when you are missing less than 25 mana; at 50.0, less than 75. Success says 'You enter a meditative trance.' and failure 'You cannot focus your concentration.' Either way you cannot use another skill for 10 seconds.

The trance ends when your mana is full ('You are at peace.') and at once if you move, swing or shoot, cast, use a skill or an item, pick something up, craft, take damage or are revealed ('You stop meditating.').
# Armor

Cloth and leather cost you nothing. Studded and hide leather count for half. Every other armor counts in full, and so does a shield: each piece adds seconds to the wait for every point of mana. A plate chest alone adds about 3.5 seconds, a wooden shield about 2, a heater shield about 6, and a full suit of plate slows every point to 7 seconds outside a trance, whatever your skill. Casting itself is not slowed by armor.
# Training it

Meditation trains in two ways. Whenever your mana is below full and you are not in a trance, each point you regain is a chance to learn, a little better the lower your mana is. And a successful trance is one more chance. The chances are not rolled during a trance, so a trance gets mana back sooner but trains less than waiting does.

So run your mana down (every cast trains Magery and Evaluating Intelligence at the same time), then let it come back with leather or cloth on your body. Use the trance when you want the mana sooner, and try it while you are missing little mana if your skill is low. It teaches until 100.0. A mage or the mage guildmaster in Britain teaches it for 1 gold per 0.1 point, up to a third of its own skill: about 20 to 33 (see Training in the Welcome guide, [Welcome). A Pure Mage does not start with it.
# What you need
Nothing to carry. A Spellbook may stay in your hand. Wear cloth or leather: a robe, a leather cap and leather armor are fine.
# Good to know

Using Meditation reveals you if you were hidden.
Meditation also feeds Reactive Armor, whose strength is (Magery + Meditation + Inscription) / 3, and Protection.
Mana comes back whether you meditate or not; the trance only speeds it up.
# What it is
Resisting Spells is your defence against other casters. You never switch it on: it works each time a hostile spell reaches you.
# What it does

First, a chance to resist. When a harmful spell with a resist roll lands on you (Magic Arrow, Harm, Fireball, Poison, Lightning, Mana Drain, Mind Blast, Paralyze, Energy Bolt, Explosion, Flamestrike, Mana Vampire, Chain Lightning, Meteor Swarm), you throw it off with a chance that rises with your skill and falls with the caster's Magery and the spell's circle. Against a caster with 100.0 Magery:
Resisting Spells 100.0: about 40 in 100 against a first-circle spell, 35 against a third, 30 against a fifth, 25 against a seventh, 22 against an eighth
75.0: 27 in 100 down to 10
50.0: 15 in 100 down to 5
25.0: 2 or 3 in 100
0.0: never
A weaker caster is resisted more: with 50.0 Magery the 100.0 line becomes about 45 in 100 down to 27.

What a resist does: damage is cut to three quarters (Flamestrike to three fifths, Mind Blast, Chain Lightning and Meteor Swarm to one half), Poison does nothing, Paralyze lasts three quarters as long. Mana Drain and Mana Vampire are resisted 99 and 98 times in 100 whatever your skill. You are told 'You feel yourself resisting magical energy.'

Second, your skill is set against the caster's Evaluating Intelligence in Magic Arrow, Harm, Fireball, Lightning, Mind Blast, Energy Bolt, Explosion, Flamestrike, Chain Lightning and Meteor Swarm: each point of yours above it takes 0.5 percent off the damage, and each point below it lets 0.2 percent more through. That works even when the spell is not resisted.
It does not stop Clumsy, Feeblemind, Weaken, Curse or Mass Curse, the damage of Earthquake, or weapons. Standing in a Fire Field has its own small check: it cuts the damage from 2 to 1.
# Training it

It trains only when a harmful spell is cast at you, and for most spells only up to a limit set by the spell's circle: 35 for the first, then 45, 55, 65, 75, 85, 120 and 130. So Magic Arrow stops teaching at 35.0, Harm at 45.0, Fireball and Poison at 55.0, Lightning and Mana Drain at 65.0, Paralyze and Mind Blast at 75.0, Energy Bolt and Explosion at 85.0. Only the seventh-circle spells (Flamestrike, Mana Vampire, Chain Lightning, Meteor Swarm) take you on to 100.0. Curse and Mass Curse have no limit: each fresh curse trains it all the way to 100.0.

While you have exactly 0.0 most spells teach nothing, because with no skill they give you no resist chance to roll. Mana Drain, Mana Vampire, Curse and Mass Curse still teach. Standing in a Fire Field teaches too, until 30.0.

The spells come from monsters that cast, such as evil mages, orcish mages and ratman mages, or from another player. You can also cast a harmful spell at yourself. Mana Drain on yourself is one way: it needs Magery 30 from a book (10 from a scroll), costs 11 mana and a Black Pearl, a Mandrake Root and a Spider's Silk, is resisted 99 times in 100, and teaches until 65.0.

paragraphs.text: Another player may cast a harmful spell at you only if you have Criminal Intent on, you are a criminal or a murderer, you are already fighting that player, or you are at guild war with them (see Fighting other players in the Welcome guide, [Welcome).

paragraphs: A mage, the mage guildmaster or the Rangers' Guildmaster in Britain teaches it for 1 gold per 0.1 point, up to a third of its own skill: about 21 to 33 (see Training in the Welcome guide, [Welcome). A Pure Mage starts with 35.0 and a Warlock with 24.0.
# What you need
Nothing: no tool, no reagent. For Mana Drain on yourself, a Spellbook and its three reagents.
# Good to know

A resisted spell still counts as a hit: the damage that gets through can ruin the spell you are casting, and a poison that was not resisted keeps hurting until it wears off or you cure it.
Wearing armor does not change a resist.
# What it is

Spirit Speak lets you understand the dead. A ghost can talk, but to the living its words come out as a jumble of 'o' and 'O'. While you are in contact with the netherworld you read them as they were said.
# How to use it

Open your skills window and click the small button beside Spirit Speak. If it works you are told 'You establish contact with the netherworld.' and you understand every ghost you hear. The contact lasts 1.8 seconds for each point of your skill, never less than 15 seconds: 45 seconds at 25.0, 90 at 50.0, 3 minutes at 100.0. When it ends you are told 'You feel your contacts with the netherworld fade.'

Your chance of success is your skill in percent. A failure says 'You fail your attempt at contacting the netherworld.' and also cuts any contact you already had. A success while you are in contact adds no time, so use it again only after the contact has faded. It costs nothing, reveals you if you were hidden, and you must wait a second between uses. You cannot use it while dead, and a ghost needs no skill to understand other ghosts.
Hearing ghosts is all it does here.
# Training it
Use it, over and over: there is nothing to buy and no risk. It teaches until 100.0.

A healer in Britain teaches it for 1 gold per 0.1 point, up to a third of its own skill: about 27 to 33 for the healer, 22 to 29 for the healer guildmaster (see Training in the Welcome guide, [Welcome).
# What you need
Nothing: no tool, no reagent.
# Good to know

Its only use here is to understand ghosts, and a dead player understands other ghosts without it.
The Dying page of the Welcome guide, [Welcome, explains what happens when you die.
# What it is

Alchemy is the skill of making potions. You grind a reagent into an empty bottle with a Mortar and Pestle and the bottle becomes a potion: healing, curing, refreshing, strength, agility, night sight, poison or explosion.
# How to make a potion

Double-click a Mortar and Pestle in your pack. A cursor appears: click a reagent or an empty bottle in your pack and a menu opens (click the Mortar and Pestle itself instead to make the last potion again). The menu asks what kind of potion, then which one. It lists only what you have the skill and the materials to make, so a beginner sees a short list that grows as the skill rises.

Each potion uses one empty bottle and the reagent for its kind (some use several, see the table below), all in your pack. If you fail you lose half of the reagents, rounded up (all of them when the potion uses only one), but you keep the bottle. Every attempt, good or bad, wears the Mortar and Pestle a little, and a worn-out one has to be replaced.
# Training it

Every potion has a skill range, the two numbers in the table. Below the first number you cannot make it. From there your chance of success rises evenly to certain at the second number; a potion whose second number is above 100 is never quite certain, even for a Grandmaster. A number below 0 is a head start: with Alchemy at 0 you already succeed part of the time. You only learn from a potion while your skill is between its two numbers, so keep making the best potion you can; once you are past a potion's second number it no longer teaches you.
# Good to know
A Mortar and Pestle costs about 8 gold from an alchemist, or anyone with the Tinkering skill can make one from 3 iron ingots (Tinkering 20 to 70). Alchemists also sell the reagents and empty bottles.

Reagents are what Magery spells burn too, so a few of each are worth carrying. A heal potion will not heal you while you are poisoned, and you must wait 10 seconds between heal potions: cure the poison first.
# What it is
Blacksmithing (Blacksmithy in your skills window) forges armor, shields and weapons from iron ingots, repairs your metal gear and melts it down again. Better metals make better armor.
# How to make something

Stand within 2 tiles of an anvil and a forge (the smithies in Britain have both), with iron ingots and Tongs or a Smith's Hammer in your pack (a Sledge Hammer works too). Double-click the tool: the game tells you to target the tool to make your last item, or anything else to begin. Target your pile of ingots.

A menu asks what you would like to do: Repair, Smelt, Build Armor, Build Shield or Build Weapons. Armor splits into ring, chain and plate (helmets are with the plate), weapons into blades, axes, pole arms and bludgeoning weapons. Each line shows the item and its ingot cost, and only items your skill and ingots allow are listed. An attempt takes about a second and a quarter. The menu does not open again afterwards: to make the same thing again, double-click the tool and target the tool itself.
# Training it

Every recipe has two numbers in the table below. At the first your chance of success is 0%; it rises evenly to 100% at the second. A first number below 0 is a head start: at skill 0 you already succeed some of the time. You only learn while your skill is between the two numbers, so make the hardest thing you can still sometimes finish. Training works only while the skill is set to Up (see Skill locks 101 in [Welcome).

A failure costs about half the ingots (rounded up) and one use of the tool; a success costs all of them. Start with the Dagger, the cheapest thing to fail at. Make shields until about 25, then ring and chain armor, maces and swords until about 50, then plate pieces, beginning with the gorget and gloves, which cost the fewest ingots. Near the top, plate armor is what still teaches you.

Shops pay little: a Buckler sells for about 25 gold while its ingots cost about 50. Smelt your practice pieces to get about half the ingots back, and mine your own ore. Armorers, Weaponsmiths and Blacksmiths in Britain teach the basics for gold (see Training in [Welcome).
# What you need

Tongs cost about 13 gold and a Smith's Hammer about 21 at a Blacksmith, who also sells iron ingots for about 5 gold each (only 16 on the shelf to start with). Tinkering makes both tools. Every attempt, good or bad, uses one charge of the tool: a bought or newly made one has between 25 and 75, an exceptional one 100, and it breaks when they are gone.

Ore comes from Mining. Double-click ore and target a forge to smelt it into ingots. Smelting is a Mining skill check: with iron ore it cannot succeed below Mining 25 and is certain from 75, and a failure burns away half the pile.
# Special metals

Besides iron there are eight metals. You need at least this much Blacksmithing to forge with each, and this much Mining to smelt its ore: Dull Copper 65, Shadow Iron 70, Copper 75, Bronze 80, Gold 85, Agapite 90, Verite 95, Valorite 99. When the tool asks for ingots, target a pile of that metal. Armor made from them protects more, from 2 more armor rating for Dull Copper up to 16 more for Valorite, rising 2 for each step; a shield gains in proportion to your Parry skill. Metal does nothing for a weapon here, so do not spend it on one.
# Repair and Smelt

Repair: choose it, then target a metal weapon or armor piece in your pack (you still need the anvil and forge). It costs no materials, but a try can wear the item's maximum durability down for good, by 3 points at low skill, 2 from skill 70 and 1 from skill 90, and it is more likely the more damaged the item is. An item repaired too often is refused. A weapon with poison on it cannot be repaired.

Smelt: choose it, then target a metal weapon or armor piece. You get back half the ingots it cost (rounded down) if a player made it, or one ingot if not (a piece bought in a shop, for example). Pieces of special metal need the Mining skill for that metal.
# Exceptional pieces and maker's marks

When your chance of success is above 60% a piece can come out exceptional. The chance is your success chance minus 60%, easing to minus 45% between skill 95 and 100. Exceptional armor protects 8 more (a shield's share depends on Parry), exceptional weapons hit 20% harder, both last 20% longer, and shops pay a quarter more. At 100.0 Blacksmithing the game asks whether to place your maker's mark on an exceptional piece: CONTINUE puts your name on it, CANCEL leaves it plain.
# Bulk order deeds

A Blacksmith shopkeeper (not the guildmaster) offers bulk order deeds to anyone with Blacksmithy above 0: click him once and choose Bulk Order Info. A small deed asks for 10, 15 or 20 pieces of one armor or weapon type you can make. Above skill 70 it may also demand exceptional pieces, and for armor a special metal. Double-click the deed, choose Combine this deed with the item requested and target each finished piece; then drop the full deed on a Blacksmith for gold, fame and sometimes a reward item. From skill 70.1 you may be offered a large deed instead: it names several different pieces, and you fill it by combining completed small deeds into it. You can ask again after 1 hour (skill 50 or below), 2 hours (above 50) or 6 hours (above 70), in real time. Tailors and Weaponsmiths do not offer bulk orders here.
# Good to know
If the menu offers only Repair and Smelt, you lack the skill or the ingots to build anything, or you targeted a metal you cannot work yet.

paragraphs.text: A new Blacksmith starts with Tongs, Pickaxes and a large stack of iron ingots. Starter tools work for 50 attempts. Starter items are newbied (see [Welcome): they stay with you when you die, and shopkeepers will not buy them.
Mining repeats on the rock you chose until it runs dry. Walking, casting, fighting, being hurt or using another skill ends it.

paragraphs: # What it is
Bowcraft and Fletching (Bowcraft/Fletching in your skills window) makes bows and crossbows, and the arrows and bolts they shoot, from logs or boards and feathers. It also makes kindling.
# How to make something

Double-click Fletcher's Tools: the game tells you to target the tools to make your last item, or anything else to begin. Target logs, boards, feathers or shafts in your pack (if you target some other item, the game asks again). A menu asks what you would like to make: Kindling, Shafts, Arrows, Bolts, Bow, Crossbow or Heavy Crossbow, showing only what your skill and materials allow. An attempt takes about a second and a quarter. The menu does not open again afterwards: to make the same thing again, double-click the tools and target the tools themselves.
# Training it

Fletching starts you at 50%: at a recipe's first number your chance is already 50%, and it rises evenly to 100% at the second. You only learn while your skill is between a recipe's two numbers, and only while the skill is set to Up (see Skill locks 101 in [Welcome). Shafts, arrows and bolts teach to about 40, a Bow to about 70, a Crossbow to 100, and a Heavy Crossbow all the way to the top.

Shafts, arrows and bolts are made by the pile. Shafts use every log and board in your pack and its bags at once, and arrows and bolts use every shaft and feather pair you carry. The whole batch succeeds or fails together, a failure loses about half the materials, and a big pile is only one chance to learn. To train on them, carry only a handful of logs, shafts and feathers and keep the rest in the bank.

From about 30 make Bows, then Crossbows from about 60 and Heavy Crossbows from about 80. A Bow takes 7 logs and sells for about 17 gold, a Crossbow takes 7 and sells for about 25, a Heavy Crossbow takes 10 and sells for about 27. Boards cost about 3 gold each, so chop your own logs to come out ahead. A Bowyer in Britain teaches the basics for gold (see Training in [Welcome).
# What you need

Fletcher's Tools cost about 2 gold at a Bowyer. Each attempt, good or bad, uses one charge of the tools: a bought or newly made set has between 25 and 75, and then it breaks. Logs come from trees (see Lumberjacking). With an axe in your hand, use it on a pile of logs to cut boards; boards work the same as logs and weigh 1 stone instead of 2. A Carpenter sells boards for about 3 gold. A Bowyer sells feathers for about 2 gold, and a bird you carve with a knife leaves feathers on its corpse. Bowyers and Provisioners also sell finished arrows for about 2 gold and bolts for 3 to 5.
# Exceptional weapons

A Bow or Crossbow can come out exceptional: the chance is half your chance of success minus 10%, so at most 40%. An exceptional one hits 20% harder and lasts 20% longer, and at 100.0 skill the game offers a maker's mark. Shafts, arrows and bolts have no quality.
# Good to know
Kindling takes one log each and lights a campfire when you double-click it (see the Camping page).

paragraphs.text: A new Bowyer starts with Fletcher's Tools that work for 50 attempts, boards and feathers. Bulk supplies are trimmed at the start if they would be too heavy to carry. Starter items are newbied (see [Welcome): they stay with you when you die, and shopkeepers will not buy them.
Lumberjacking repeats on the tree you chose until it runs dry. Walking, casting, fighting, being hurt or using another skill ends it.

paragraphs: # What it is

Carpentry makes furniture, chests, boxes and crates, wooden shields and staves, musical instruments, barrel parts and house add-on deeds (beds, forges, anvils, looms, spinning wheels, ovens and more) from logs or boards.
# How to make something

Double-click a Saw, or another carpentry tool (Dovetail Saw, Hammer, Draw Knife, Froe, Inshave, Scorp, Nails or a plane): the game tells you to target the tool to make your last item, or anything else to begin. Target logs or boards in your pack. A menu offers Furniture, Containers, Weapons, Instruments, Miscellaneous and Add-Ons. Each opens a list that shows the wood an item takes and holds only what your skills and materials allow. An attempt takes about a second and a quarter. The menu does not open again afterwards: to make the same thing again, double-click the tool and target the tool itself.
# Training it

Carpentry starts you at 50%: at a recipe's first number your chance is already 50%, rising evenly to 100% at the second. Every recipe teaches over a 25-point stretch, so you move on from one item to the next, and only while the skill is set to Up (see Skill locks 101 in [Welcome). Begin with barrel staves, then small crates, stools and wooden boxes. A wooden shield (9 logs) is a cheap teacher from about 53, a quarterstaff (6 logs) from about 74, and a shepherd's crook or gnarled staff (7 logs) from about 79, which keeps teaching to the top.

Shops pay little: a wooden shield sells for about 15 gold, a shepherd's crook 10, a quarterstaff 9, a stool 6. Chop your own logs and the wood is free. A Carpenter in Britain teaches the basics for gold (see Training in [Welcome).
# What you need

A Saw costs about 15 gold at a Carpenter, who also sells boards for about 3 gold and most of the other tools. Tinkering makes saws, planes and most carpentry tools. Each attempt, good or bad, uses one charge of the tool: a bought or newly made one has between 25 and 75, and then it breaks. Logs come from trees (see Lumberjacking). With an axe in your hand, use it on a pile of logs to cut boards; boards work the same as logs and weigh 1 stone instead of 2.
# Boxes, kegs and add-ons

A wooden box, crate or chest you make may come with a lock and key if you also have some Tinkering: the better your Tinkering, the harder the lock is to pick. A keg takes 3 barrel staves, a barrel lid and barrel hoops (hoops are a Tinkering part), and Tinkering turns a keg into a potion keg. Add-on deeds are for houses: double-click the deed and pick a spot inside a house you own. Instruments, the fishing pole and many add-ons also need a second skill (between 40 and 80, depending on the item) and other materials such as cloth or ingots, and the menu lists them only when you have both.
# Exceptional pieces

Wooden shields, staves and instruments can come out exceptional: the chance is your success chance minus 60%, so at most 40%. An exceptional shield protects more, an exceptional staff hits 20% harder, and at 100.0 skill the game offers a maker's mark.

paragraphs.text: A new Carpenter starts with boards and a Saw that works for 50 attempts. Bulk supplies are trimmed at the start if they would be too heavy to carry. Starter items are newbied (see [Welcome): they stay with you when you die, and shopkeepers will not buy them.
Lumberjacking repeats on the tree you chose until it runs dry. Walking, casting, fighting, being hurt or using another skill ends it.

paragraphs: # What it is
Cartography draws maps and decodes treasure maps. In this shard it needs no tool: you use the skill itself and spend blank maps.
# How to make a map

Use the Cartography skill. A menu asks what kind of map: a map of the local environs, a map suitable for cities, a moderately sized sea chart, or a map of the world. It lists only the kinds you have the skill for, and only while you hold a blank map; if nothing is listed you have no blank map or too little skill. Each map uses one blank map and takes about a second and a quarter.

Double-click a finished map to read it. The local map, city map and sea chart show the area around the spot where you stood when you drew them, and more skill draws a wider area (the sea chart reaches farthest). The world map shows the same region wherever you draw it, and it widens with skill.
# Training it

Your chance is 0% at a recipe's first number and rises evenly to 100% at the second; you learn only in between, and only while the skill is set to Up (see Skill locks 101 in [Welcome). A local map teaches from about 10, a city map from about 25, a sea chart from about 35 and the world map from about 40, each over the next 60 points. Make the best map you can. A failed try loses the blank map.

Blank maps cost about 5 gold at a Mapmaker, who pays only 3 gold for a finished local, city or world map (and nothing for a sea chart), so training costs gold. A Mapmaker in Britain teaches the basics for gold (see Training in [Welcome).
# Treasure maps

Treasure maps turn up from fishing and, rarely, from monster loot. Double-click one to try to decode it with Cartography. A level 1 map can be tried at any skill, level 2 needs 41, level 3 needs 51, level 4 needs 61 and levels 5 and 6 need 70. A failure says you fail to make anything of the map, and you can try again.
# What you need
Blank maps: a Mapmaker sells them (there is one in Britain). A new character with Cartography starts with 4 blank maps and a sextant. You do not need a Mapmaker's Pen.
# Good to know
Maps have no quality: none is exceptional and none carries a maker's mark. Blank scrolls cannot stand in for blank maps here.
# What it is

Cooking turns raw food into cooked food you can eat. In this era there is no cooking tool and no cooking menu: you use the raw food itself on a fire. The skillets, rolling pins and flour sifters that cooks sell open no menu here, and flour, dough and baking are not part of this shard's cooking.
# How to cook

Double-click the raw food (it must be in your pack, or within 2 tiles), then target a fire within 1 tile of you: a campfire, an oven or fireplace, a fire pit, a heating stand, a Fire Field spell, or a small or large forge. After 5 seconds your Cooking skill decides. On success the cooked food goes into your pack; on failure it burns to a crisp and is lost. Walk more than 3 tiles from the fire during those 5 seconds and it burns too. One piece cooks at a time, even from a stack, and trying again too soon says you must wait.

Raw ribs, lamb legs, chicken legs, birds and fish steaks all cook this way, each into its cooked form. For a fire, double-click Kindling to light a campfire beside you (a Camping skill roll; a Provisioner sells Kindling for about 2 gold). The baker's and the cook's shops in Britain have ovens, and its smithies have forges.
# Training it

Your chance is your Cooking skill as a percentage: at skill 50 half your tries succeed. Every raw food can be tried at any skill and teaches the same, so cook whatever is cheapest, from the start up to the top. Training works only while the skill is set to Up (see Skill locks 101 in [Welcome).

Raw food costs more than the cooked food sells for. A Butcher sells raw chicken legs for about 6 gold, birds for 9, lamb legs for 9 and ribs for 16, while a Cook pays about 3 for a cooked chicken leg, 8 for a cooked bird and 4 for a cooked lamb leg. Cooking is for training and eating, not earning. Cheaper raw food: carve a dead animal with a knife (ribs, lamb legs and birds), or carve a fish you caught with a knife or sword for four raw fish steaks. A Cook or Herbalist in Britain teaches the basics for gold (see Training in [Welcome).
# Eating

Double-click cooked food to eat it. It fills your hunger and gives back a little stamina; when you are full the game says you are too full to eat more. Poisoned food poisons whoever eats it (see Poisoning).
# Good to know
Cooked food has no quality: every attempt takes the same 5 seconds, and only one can run at a time.

paragraphs.text: A new cook starts with raw lamb legs, chicken legs and fish steaks, Kindling, a flour sack and a pitcher (the flour sack and pitcher have no use in cooking here). Bulk supplies are trimmed at the start if they would be too heavy to carry. Starter items are newbied (see [Welcome): they stay with you when you die, and shopkeepers will not buy them.

One click is enough for a whole stack: the game cooks each piece in turn at the fire you chose, burned or not, until the stack is gone. Walking, casting, using another skill, war mode, fighting or being hurt ends it.

paragraphs: # What it is

Inscription writes spell scrolls from blank scrolls, reagents and your own mana, copies books, and makes Runebooks. You can only scribe a spell that is in a spellbook you carry. It needs no tool in this shard.
# How to scribe a scroll

Use the Inscription skill. The game asks you to target the book you wish to copy or the scroll you want to use: target a blank scroll in your pack (you have a minute to choose). A menu asks Which circle of spells? and lists the Runebook and the first to eighth circles, then Which spell would you like to scribe? Only spells you can scribe now are listed: the spell must be in a spellbook you carry, your skill must reach it, and you need a blank scroll and every reagent it takes. The menu does not open again afterwards: use the skill again for the next scroll.

Scribing also costs the spell's mana: 4, 6, 9, 11, 14, 20, 40 and 50 for circles one to eight, taken only when the scroll works. If it fails, the scroll is ruined and the reagents are lost, but your mana is kept. The seventh and eighth circles need a mana pool of 40 and 50.
# Runebooks and copies

A Runebook takes 8 blank scrolls, a Recall scroll, a Gate Travel scroll and an unmarked recall rune (a Mage sells runes for about 15 gold). Pick Runebook in the menu, or target a recall rune at the first prompt. To copy a book, target the book with writing in it and then a writable book: it is a skill check and uses no materials.
# Training it

Every scroll has two numbers in the table below. At the first your chance is 0%, rising evenly to 100% at the second, and you learn only in between, and only while the skill is set to Up (see Skill locks 101 in [Welcome). Each circle starts about 14 points higher than the one before: the first circle can be tried at skill 0, the third from about 4, the fifth from about 32, the seventh from about 61 and the eighth from 75, and each teaches over a 50-point stretch. Scribe the highest circle you can.

Spells that need one reagent are the cheapest: Magic Arrow (sulfurous ash), Fireball (black pearl) and Poison (nightshade) among the early ones. A blank scroll costs about 5 gold and a reagent about 3 (5 for black pearl and bloodmoss), so a scroll costs roughly 8 to 20 gold to make, while a Mage shop pays only 4 to 18 gold for one. Scribe for yourself and for other players, not for the shops. A Mage or Scribe in Britain teaches the basics for gold (see Training in [Welcome).
You need the spells in a spellbook: a Mage sells a spellbook for about 18 gold and sells scrolls of the first three circles; drop a scroll on your spellbook to add its spell.
# What you need
Blank scrolls cost about 5 gold at a Scribe or a Mage (and 12 at a Mapmaker). Mages and Alchemists sell all eight reagents. You do not need a Scribe's Pen.
# Good to know

If the menu shows no spells, one of four things is missing: the spell in a spellbook you carry, enough skill, a blank scroll, or the reagents. Check the mana last: the game tells you when you lack it.

paragraphs.text: A new Scribe starts with blank scrolls, a bag of reagents and a Scribe's Pen (not needed here). Bulk supplies are trimmed at the start if they would be too heavy to carry. Starter items are newbied (see [Welcome): they stay with you when you die, and shopkeepers will not buy them.

paragraphs: # What it is
Tailoring sews clothes from cloth and shoes and leather armor from leather. The leather gear covers ordinary and studded armor, with separate female cuts.
# How to make something

Double-click a Sewing Kit: the game tells you to target the kit to make your last item, or anything else to begin. Target cloth to make clothes, or leather or hides to make shoes and armor (anything else and the game asks you to select cloth, leather or hides). Cloth opens Build Hats, Build Shirts, Build Pants and Build Misc. Leather opens Build Shoes, Build Leather Armor, Build Studded Armor and Build Female Armor. Each line shows the item and what it takes, and only items your skill and materials allow are listed. An attempt takes about a second and a quarter. The menu does not open again afterwards: to make the same thing again, double-click the kit and target the kit itself.
Cloth of different colors does not mix. The cloth you target decides the color: only cloth of exactly that color is used, and the new garment takes that color. Keep each color in its own pile.
# Training it

Tailoring starts you at 50%: at a recipe's first number your chance is already 50%, rising evenly to 100% at the second. You only learn between a recipe's two numbers, and only while the skill is set to Up (see Skill locks 101 in [Welcome).

Begin with skull caps and bandanas (2 cloth) or a leather cap (2 leather), then sandals and shoes. From about 52 make leather gloves (3 leather) and gorgets (4), then sleeves, leggings and a tunic. From about 79 the studded gorget (6 leather) is the cheapest piece that still teaches, and studded armor teaches to the top. Cloth items (shirts, dresses, cloaks, robes) teach up to about 79.

Shops pay little for clothes, but a Tanner pays about 30 gold for leather gloves, 37 for a gorget and 40 for sleeves, more than the leather costs (about 6 gold each at a Tanner). Hides count as leather in the menu. A Tailor in Britain teaches the basics for gold (see Training in [Welcome).
# What you need

A Sewing Kit costs about 3 gold at a Tailor, who also sells cloth for about 2 gold a piece. Tinkering makes sewing kits. Each attempt, good or bad, uses one charge: a bought or newly made kit has between 25 and 75, and then it breaks. A failed attempt with leather costs about half of it (rounded up).

Leather comes from hides: carve a dead animal with a knife and the hides are left on the corpse. Double-click scissors and target a pile of hides to turn the whole pile into leather, which weighs 1 stone instead of 5. A Tanner sells leather. Cloth comes from bolts: scissors cut a bolt of cloth into 50 pieces. A loom weaves 5 yarn or thread into a bolt, and a spinning wheel spins wool, cotton or flax into yarn or thread. Britain's weavers and tailors have wheels and looms.
# Recycling
Scissors on clothing or leather armor that a player made give back half the cloth or leather it took. On a shop-bought piece you get 1.
# Exceptional pieces and maker's marks

Leather armor can come out exceptional when your chance of success is above 60%. The chance is your success chance minus 60%, easing to minus 45% between skill 95 and 100. Exceptional armor protects 8 more and lasts 20% longer. Exceptional clothing is only labelled. At 100.0 Tailoring the game asks whether to place your maker's mark on an exceptional piece.
# Good to know
The menu works with ordinary cloth, leather and hides. Tailors and Weavers do not give bulk orders here.

paragraphs.text: A new Tailor starts with cloth, leather and a Sewing Kit that works for 50 attempts. Bulk supplies are trimmed at the start if they would be too heavy to carry. Starter items are newbied (see [Welcome): they stay with you when you die, and shopkeepers will not buy them.
Every new character starts with a pair of scissors that is bound to you for good.

A spinning wheel spins your whole stack of wool, cotton or flax from one click, and a loom takes your whole stack of yarn or thread at once. Walking, casting, using another skill, war mode, fighting or being hurt ends it.

paragraphs: # What it is

Tinkering makes tools, parts, utensils, simple traps, jewelry and small wooden and metal goods, from iron ingots or logs. Its best use is making the tools other crafts run on: Tongs, Sewing Kits, saws, pickaxes, Mortars and Pestles and more.
# How to make something

Double-click Tinker's Tools: the game tells you to target the tools to make your last item, or anything else to begin. Target what you want to work with: iron ingots (a menu of Tools, Parts, Utensils, Traps, Miscellaneous and Jewelry, and Wooden Items if you also carry logs), logs or boards (the wooden items), or a keg (the potion keg). Each line shows the item and what it takes, and only items your skill and materials allow are listed. An attempt takes about a second and a quarter. The menu does not open again afterwards: to make the same thing again, double-click the tools and target the tools themselves.
# Training it

Every recipe has two numbers in the table below. At the first your chance of success is 0% (the potion keg starts at 50%), rising evenly to 100% at the second, and you learn only in between, and only while the skill is set to Up (see Skill locks 101 in [Welcome).

The cheapest teachers take one ingot: forks, spoons and table knives teach from 0 to about 50 (Utensils), Hammers from about 30, Tongs from about 35 and Lockpicks from about 45 up to 95. Gears, springs, hinges, scissors, Tinker's Tools and Sewing Kits take two ingots and teach between 5 and 70. Past 55 make Candelabras, Globes, Scales, Spyglasses and Heating Stands (4 ingots each), and from 75 potion kegs (a keg, 10 empty bottles, a barrel lid and a barrel tap).

Hammers sell best: a Carpenter pays about 14 gold for one that cost a single ingot (about 5 gold). Tongs sell for about 7 gold to a Blacksmith, a Smith's Hammer for 10, a saw for 9 to a Carpenter, scissors for 6 to a Tailor.
A Tinker or the Tinkers' Guildmaster in Britain teaches Tinkering for 1 gold per 0.1 point, up to a third of their own skill: about 21 to 33 (see Training in [Welcome).
# What you need

Tinker's Tools: the Tinker in Britain sells them for about 7 gold (20 on the shelf), and you can make another set yourself, so keep a spare. Each attempt, good or bad, uses one charge: a set has between 25 and 75 when made or bought, and 100 if it was made exceptional. Ingots cost about 5 gold at a Blacksmith (only 16 on the shelf to start with) or come from your own ore (see Mining and Blacksmithing). Logs are for the wooden items.
# Tools for other crafts

The Tools list holds the tools of the other crafts: Tongs, Smith's Hammer and Sledge Hammer for Blacksmithing, the Sewing Kit for Tailoring, saws, Hammer, Draw Knife, Froe, Inshave and Scorp (and the planes, in the wooden items) for Carpentry, the Mortar and Pestle for Alchemy, Pickaxe, Shovel and Hatchet for gathering, plus Scissors and Lockpicks.
# Traps and jewelry

A dart, poison or explosion trap takes an ingot plus a bolt, a poison potion or an explosion potion. After you make one, the game asks what to set it on: target a lockable chest that you can reach, that is unlocked, not locked down and has no trap yet. The trap stays off until you lock the chest, and it grows stronger with your Tinkering.

Necklaces, earrings and rings (and a wedding ring) take 2 ingots each and a gem. The game asks you to target a gemstone: the whole stack you target is set into the piece and names it, so split off a single gem first. Jewelers sell gems.
# Exceptional tools

Tools you make can come out exceptional when your chance of success is above 60%: the chance is your success chance minus 60%, so at most 40%. An exceptional tool has 100 uses instead of 25 to 75. At 100.0 Tinkering the game offers a maker's mark.
# Good to know
The Tinkering menu has no Repair.

paragraphs.text: A Tinker may also be able to make the Backpack Ward: if the recipe is on offer, it is in the Miscellaneous list and the table shows what it takes. A Ward has no quality, so it is never exceptional.

A new Tinker starts with Tinker's Tools that work for 50 attempts and a stack of iron ingots. Starter items are newbied (see [Welcome): they stay with you when you die, and shopkeepers will not buy them.

paragraphs: # What it is
Poisoning puts a poison potion on a weapon or on food. A poisoned blade may poison what it hits, and poisoned food poisons whoever eats it. The skill makes nothing new: it spends poison potions.
# How to use it

Use the Poisoning skill (you can use it once every 10 seconds). The game says to select the poison you wish to use: target a poison potion in your pack. It then asks what to apply the poison to: target a weapon or a piece of food. After about 2 seconds your Poisoning skill decides. The potion is used up either way, and you get the empty bottle back.
Only a one-handed weapon with a blade or a point can be poisoned (it does not have to be in your hand). Axes, maces, bows and two-handed weapons cannot, and the game says so if you try.

A poisoned weapon carries charges: 18 for a Lesser poison, 16 for Regular, 14 for Greater and 12 for Deadly. Each hit with a poisoned sword, dagger or spear uses one charge and has a 50% chance to poison the target. Poison on food stays until someone eats it.
# Training it

Each potion has its own skill range: Lesser 0 to 60, Regular 30 to 70, Greater 60 to 100, Deadly 95 to 100. Your chance is 0% at the first number and rises evenly to 100% at the second, and you learn only in between, and only while the skill is set to Up (see Skill locks 101 in [Welcome). Below the first number a potion always fails. Use the strongest potion you can still sometimes get on: a harder try is more likely to teach you something.
The Thieves' Guildmaster in Britain teaches Poisoning for 1 gold per 0.1 point, up to a third of its own skill: about 20 to 28 (see Training in [Welcome).

Every try spends a potion. Apply the poison to a single piece of cheap food or to a dagger you do not mind (a whole stack of food is poisoned together). Below 80 Poisoning, a failed try has a 1 in 20 chance of poisoning you, so keep Cure potions.

Brew your own potions with Alchemy (a Lesser poison potion is one nightshade and an empty bottle, and nightshade costs about 3 gold) or buy Lesser potions from an Alchemist or a Mage for about 15 gold. The empty bottles come back to you, so keep them.
# Good to know
Each success costs you 20 karma.
A weapon with poison on it cannot be repaired, and an oil cloth does not wipe poison off a weapon in this shard: the poison only goes as the charges are used up.
A new character with Poisoning starts with 2 Lesser poison potions.

paragraphs.text: Every new character starts with 5 Lesser Cure potions, which cure a Lesser poison most of the time. If a failed try poisons you, drink one.

paragraphs: # What it is

Mining is digging ore out of mountains and cave walls with a Pickaxe or a Shovel. Ore is raw metal: you smelt it at a forge into ingots, and blacksmiths and tinkers turn ingots into weapons, armor and tools. Mining also decides which metals you can smelt.
# How to use it

Double-click a Pickaxe or Shovel (in your pack or in your hand), then click a mountainside or a cave wall within 2 tiles of you, with a clear line of sight. A dig takes less than a second.
