You cannot dig while riding a mount or while changed into another shape by a spell, so get off your mount first. Each ore you dig uses one use of the tool (a new Pickaxe or Shovel has 50), and a used-up tool is gone. A miss costs no use.

paragraphs.text: Mining repeats on the spot you chose until that patch runs dry, at the usual dig time. Walking, casting, using another skill, entering war mode, fighting or being hurt, or opening another gathering target stops it. A full pack or a used-up tool stops it too. If you target something new while it runs, it moves on to that once the current dig finishes.

paragraphs: # Where the ore is

The mountains are divided into patches 8 tiles wide and 8 deep. A patch holds 10 to 34 ore at a time, and one good dig gives one ore. When a patch is empty you are told there is no metal here to mine. It refills 10 to 20 minutes after the first ore was taken from it, so move to the next patch and come back later.
Every patch has one kind of metal, and it never changes. About half of all patches are plain iron. The rest hold a better metal, and each better metal is rarer than the one before it.

Mining skill you need for each metal (the skill you have trained):
Iron: any
Dull Copper: 65
Shadow Iron: 70
Copper: 75
Bronze: 80
Gold: 85
Agapite: 90
Verite: 95
Valorite: 99

Each dig in a better patch is first an even toss between iron and the better metal. The better metal then has a skill check of its own: even odds at the skill listed, and a little easier with each extra point. So at the listed skill about 1 dig in 4 gives the better metal, and the rest give iron or nothing. With less skill than a metal needs, a patch of that metal gives only iron. In an iron patch your chance on each dig is about your Mining in percent.
# Ore and smelting

Ore comes in three sizes, and ore of different sizes does not stack. About 3 in 4 pieces are large (12 stones each), and the rest are medium (7) or small (2). Ore is heavy, so smelt it soon. Double-click ore and click a forge within 2 tiles of you (look for one in a blacksmith's shop). A large ore makes 2 ingots, a medium ore 1, and a small one half an ingot, so a single small ore makes none. An ingot weighs a tenth of a stone. To join two piles of the same metal, double-click one and click the other.

Smelting is a Mining skill check, made once for the whole pile. For iron your chance is nil at about Mining 25, even at about 50 and certain at about 75, and a failed smelt burns away half of the pile. Colored ore needs the Mining of its metal (65 and up, as listed above) just to try; with less you are told you have no idea how to smelt it. At that skill the chance is even, and it is certain 25 points higher.
# Training it

Dig iron anywhere to start, and leave the ore unsmelted until Mining is about 25, because a failed smelt halves the pile. From about 25 to 75 smelt your iron as well: smelting trains Mining too. Iron is never certain until Mining 100, so it teaches you the whole way. From 65 on, work patches that give colored ore: the better metal is harder to find, and a harder try teaches more. If you only ever dig iron at 65 or more, move to another patch.

A trainer saves time at the start: the miner or the miner guildmaster in Britain teaches Mining up to about 22 to 33, for 1 gold per 0.1 point (see Training in [Welcome). Make sure the arrow beside the skill in your skills window is set to Up, or it will not gain (see Skill locks 101 in [Welcome).
# What you need

A Pickaxe costs about 22 gold from a blacksmith, and a character created with Mining skill starts with one. The Miner and the Tinker in Britain sell a Shovel for about 12 gold (and a Pickaxe for 25). You can also make a Pickaxe or a Shovel yourself with Tinker's Tools, from 4 iron ingots (Tinkering 40 to 90). A blacksmith pays 4 gold for each iron ingot. Ore is heavy, and your Strength sets how much you can carry: 40 stones plus 3.5 for each point of Strength.
# Good to know
To dig up the chest on a treasure map you need a Shovel in your pack. A Pickaxe does not count for that.

paragraphs.text: Fire Island, the Buccaneer's Den island and the Hythloth dungeon are Hot Zones, where players can attack each other freely, so dig with care there. Everywhere else the Criminal Intent rules in [Welcome decide who can fight you.

paragraphs: # What it is

Lumberjacking is chopping trees for logs. Carpenters and bowyers build from logs and the boards you cut from them. The skill also makes you hit harder with an axe: 1 percent more damage for every 5 points, 20 percent at 100. Hitting with an axe trains it too.
# How to use it

Hold an axe in your hand. A Hatchet is the cheapest; most larger axes work too (not the war axe), and so do a bardiche and a halberd (those two are used up after 150 good chops). Double-click it and click a tree within 2 tiles of you, in sight. If the axe is not in your hand you are told it must be equipped. A try is one to three swings, from 1 to 4 seconds in all and about 2.5 on average.

A good chop gives 10 logs; a miss gives nothing. Each small patch of forest, 4 tiles wide and 3 deep, holds 20 to 45 wood, enough for 2 to 4 good chops. Then you are told there is not enough wood here, and the patch refills 20 to 30 minutes after the first chop. There is only one kind of wood, plain logs.

paragraphs.text: Lumberjacking repeats on the tree you chose until the wood in that patch runs out, at the usual pace. Walking, casting, using another skill, entering war mode, fighting or being hurt, or opening another gathering target stops it. A full pack stops it too.

paragraphs: # Logs, boards and Kindling

A log weighs 2 stones, so one good chop is 20 stones. To make boards, double-click your equipped axe and click a pile of logs in your pack: the whole pile turns into boards, one for one, and a board weighs 1 stone. Carpenters pay about 1 gold for a log and 2 for a board.
Kindling is wood for fires. Use a knife or a sword (not an axe) on a tree: it needs no skill, gives one Kindling and uses up 5 of the patch's wood. A Provisioner sells Kindling for 2 gold.
# Training it

Plain logs never get harder, so keep chopping from 0 to 100. Your chance on each try is about your Lumberjacking in percent: at 50 you get logs from about half your tries. Axe fighters also gain the skill as they fight with an axe. A trainer saves time at the start: the carpenter in Britain teaches Lumberjacking up to about 20 to 27, for 1 gold per 0.1 point (see Training in [Welcome). Make sure the arrow beside the skill in your skills window is set to Up, or it will not gain (see Skill locks 101 in [Welcome).
# What you need

A Hatchet costs about 25 gold from a weaponsmith. You can also make one yourself with Tinker's Tools, from 4 iron ingots (Tinkering 30 to 80). A carpenter buys your logs and boards. Your Strength sets how much you can carry: 40 stones plus 3.5 for each point. At 20 stones a chop a pack fills fast, so cut your logs into boards, which weigh half as much.
# Good to know
Kindling is also what Camping lights, so a woodcutter can keep a camper supplied.

paragraphs.text: Fire Island, the Buccaneer's Den island and the Hythloth dungeon are Hot Zones, where players can attack each other freely, so chop with care there. Everywhere else the Criminal Intent rules in [Welcome decide who can fight you.

paragraphs: # What it is

Fishing is catching fish from the water with a Fishing Pole. Fish are food: a knife, dagger or sword cuts one into 4 raw fish steaks, and Cooking turns those into meals. Shops pay only about 1 gold for a fish.
# How to use it

Double-click a Fishing Pole (in your pack or in your hands) and click water within 4 tiles of you and in sight. You cannot fish while riding. A cast takes about 8 seconds, and then you see the result: a fish, something odd, or nothing. An 8 by 8 stretch of water holds 5 to 15 catches at a time. When it is empty you are told the fish do not seem to be biting here, and it refills 10 to 20 minutes after the first catch.

paragraphs.text: Fishing repeats on the water you chose until the fish stop biting there, at the usual 8 seconds a cast. Walking, casting, using another skill, entering war mode, fighting or being hurt, or opening another gathering target stops it. A full pack stops it too.

paragraphs: # What you catch

First your skill is checked: the chance is about your Fishing in percent. Then the water decides what you pulled up. As your skill rises, more of the pulls are fish.
Fish: about 4 in 10 at skill 0, 5 in 10 at 50, 7 in 10 at 100.
Nothing (the line comes up empty): about 4 in 10 at skill 0, 1 in 4 at 100.
Footwear (boots, shoes, sandals or thigh boots): 1 in 5 at skill 0, 1 in 100 at 100.
A small rare fish: 1 in 20 at skill 0, 1 in 100 at 100.

Double-click a rare fish to swallow it. A prized fish gives +5 Intelligence, a wondrous fish +5 Dexterity and a truly rare fish +5 Strength, each for one minute. A highly peculiar fish gives 10 stamina.
# Deep water

Out on the open sea the water gives up stranger things. This works only in deep open water: the game checks the water around the spot you fish in, out to about 25 tiles along each diagonal. From Fishing 80 a pull can be a big fish (3 to 200 stones; cut up, it gives one steak for every 4 stones, and at least 4) or a Special Fishing Net, from 90 a sodden piece of parchment (a treasure map), and at 100 a message in a bottle. Each is rarer lower down, and even at 100 each is only about 1 pull in 200.

A net, a map or a bottle never arrives alone: a sea serpent appears nearby holding it (a Deep Sea Serpent one time in four), so be ready to fight for the prize. A Special Fishing Net, used in deep water, hauls up sea monsters that attack you, so do not use one unprepared.
# Training it

Ordinary water is the same at every skill, so you fish the same way from 0 to 100. At 8 seconds a cast the skill is slow, so be patient. A trainer saves time at the start: a fisherman in Britain teaches Fishing up to about 25 to 32, for 1 gold per 0.1 point (see Training in [Welcome). Make sure the arrow beside the skill in your skills window is set to Up, or it will not gain (see Skill locks 101 in [Welcome).
# What you need
A Fishing Pole costs about 15 gold from a fisherman, who also pays about 1 gold for each fish. A fish weighs 1 stone, so sell or cook what you catch.
# Good to know
The pole works from your pack. Held in your hands it takes both, so you cannot fight with a weapon in the other hand.

paragraphs.text: Fire Island, the Buccaneer's Den island and the Hythloth dungeon are Hot Zones, where players can attack each other freely, so fish with care there. Everywhere else the Criminal Intent rules in [Welcome decide who can fight you.

paragraphs: # What it is
Camping is lighting and tending a campfire. You light Kindling on a free tile next to you. A fire gives light, and near it a camp becomes secure, which lets a Bedroll log you out at once and safely.

paragraphs.text: On this shard your Camping skill also decides how long your fires burn.

paragraphs: # Lighting a fire

Double-click Kindling to light a campfire on one of the four tiles beside you (north, east, south or west). You need a clear line of sight to the tile, and you cannot light a fire inside a dungeon. A fire that lights uses one Kindling; a try that fails uses none. Fires are not saved, so a server restart puts every fire out.

paragraphs.text: Anyone can light a fire. The chance is 50 percent at Camping 50 or less and rises with your skill to 100 percent at Camping 100. Every try can train the skill.

How long a fire burns depends on the Camping skill of whoever lit it, and every point counts from the first: it burns for 100 seconds plus 2 for each point, the last third of that burning low, then smoulders as embers for 60 seconds plus 1.2 for each point, and goes out.
Camping 0: 100 seconds of fire, 160 in all.
Camping 50: 200 seconds of fire, 320 in all.
Camping 100: 300 seconds of fire, 480 in all.

Use Kindling within 1 tile of a fire to feed it instead of lighting another: its burn starts over as if you had just lit it (a fire never gets shorter), and embers flare back to life. A feed uses one Kindling and needs no skill roll, so it does not train Camping. A fire cannot be fed in the 5 seconds after it was lit or fed. To light a second fire, stand 2 tiles from the first.
# Your kit

Every new character starts with a Bedroll and 5 Kindling in the pack. They are newbied, which means they stay with you when you die. Kindling weighs 5 stones each and the Bedroll 5, so the kit is 30 stones.

paragraphs: # A secure camp and the Bedroll

Stay within 7 tiles of a burning fire. You are told it will take a few moments to secure your camp, and after 30 seconds you are told the camp is now secure. Embers do not count: if the fire falls to embers, or you walk out of the 7 tiles, the camp is no longer secure.

Being in a secure camp is what lets a Bedroll log you out. Drop the Bedroll on the ground within 2 tiles of you (it does nothing while it is in your pack). Double-click it to unroll it, then double-click it again to roll it up. In a secure camp a window then asks whether to leave; it closes by itself after 10 seconds. Choose Continue and your character leaves the world at once, with the Bedroll back in your pack. Without a Bedroll, a character that logs out in the wild stays in the world for 5 minutes.
A secure camp protects nothing else: monsters, and players where players may fight, can still attack you there.

paragraphs.text: # Camp travel

Use [CampTravel to travel to a campfire lit by another member of your party. The fire must have burned for 30 seconds and not be down to embers, and whoever lit it needs Camping 50 or more. A fire takes as many travelers as its lighter's Camping allows, counted over the fire's whole life: 1 at Camping 50, one more for each 10 points, up to 6.

The trip costs you 2 Kindling and 5 seconds standing still, and you can travel this way once every 30 minutes on your account. Criminals and murderers may use it, but nobody who attacked a player in the last 30 seconds can. It cannot be used to leave a Hot Zone (a place where players can fight freely) or a dungeon, to reach a camp inside a dungeon, or while you are Knocked Out (beaten down by another player) or overloaded. Only a bonded pet beside you would come with you, and there is no bonding on this shard, so your pets stay behind. If the camp is inside a Hot Zone you are warned first, unless you switched the warning off with [TravelWarning.

A fire you can travel to burns blue. You can have one blue fire at a time: the first fire you light keeps the blue until it burns down to embers, and any other fire you light meanwhile is an ordinary fire that nobody can travel to. A fire burns blue only if you have Camping 50 or more. You are told when your fire is blue and how many places it has.

paragraphs: # Training it

Light Kindling again and again. Each fire that lights costs one Kindling (2 gold at a Provisioner), and a failed try costs none. Stand in the open so there is a free tile beside you. Make sure the arrow beside the skill in your skills window is set to Up, or it will not gain (see Skill locks 101 in [Welcome).
The Rangers' Guildmaster in Britain teaches Camping for 1 gold per 0.1 point, up to a third of its own skill: about 25 to 33 (see Training in [Welcome).

paragraphs.text: With the 50 percent floor you light about every second try even at Camping 0. Above 50 the chance rises, and an easier try teaches less. Because a fire's length follows your real skill, every point pays at once.

paragraphs: # What you need

A Provisioner sells Kindling for 2 gold and a Bedroll for 5. You can also make Kindling from a tree: use a knife or a sword on it (see Lumberjacking). Kindling weighs 5 stones each, so carry only what you will use.
# Good to know
A burning or dimming campfire is also a heat source for cooking: double-click raw food, then click the fire from within 1 tile (see Cooking). Embers do not cook.
# What it is
Tracking finds creatures and people near you and points an arrow at the one you choose. It works on animals, monsters, human townsfolk and other players.
# How to use it

Press the button beside Tracking in your skills window. A small window asks what to track: Animals, Monsters, Human NPCs or Players. If your skill check passes, a second window lists up to 12 of that kind within range, nearest first, each with a picture and a name. Click the button under one. An arrow on your screen points toward it and keeps pointing as it moves.

Right-click the arrow to stop following. You also lose the trail, and are told you have lost your quarry, when the creature gets farther away than twice your search range or leaves the map. If none of that kind is in range you are told you see no evidence of them. You must wait 10 seconds after using Tracking before you can use it, or any other skill from your skills window, again.
# How far it sees
Your search range is 10 tiles plus 10 more for every full 10 points of Tracking: 10 tiles below 10 skill, 60 at 50 and 110 at 100. Only the 12 nearest of the kind you picked are listed.

The check to search at all is easy. Below 21.1 it can fail: its chance is your Tracking divided by 21.1, and a fail tells you that you see no evidence of those in the area. From 21.1 on it always passes.
Hiding and Stealth do not hide a player from Tracking here, but a hidden staff member never shows. Tracking tells you where something is, not how dangerous it is.
# Training it

Use it, wait 10 seconds, use it again. It trains with nobody around: once the first check passes, the skill is checked again over the range from 21.1 to 100 before the search starts, so a lone tracker trains as fast as one in a crowd. Below 21.1 the first check is the one that trains you. The 10 seconds between uses make it slow, so do something else while you wait. Make sure the arrow beside the skill in your skills window is set to Up, or it will not gain (see Skill locks 101 in [Welcome).
The Rangers' Guildmaster in Britain teaches Tracking for 1 gold per 0.1 point, up to a third of its own skill: about 30 to 33 (see Training in [Welcome).
# What you need
Nothing: Tracking needs no tool and no reagent. It is a skill you use, with a button in your skills window.
# Good to know
Track Animals to find something to tame, or Monsters to steer clear of the dangerous ones.

paragraphs.text: Finding a player shows you where they are and nothing more. Whether you may attack them is decided by the Criminal Intent rules (see Fighting other players in [Welcome).

paragraphs: # What it is

Herding moves a wild animal where you point, using a Shepherd's Crook. It does not tame the animal. It is useful for moving animals out of your way, away from a place you want to work, or to a spot you choose.
# How to use it

Double-click the crook (in your pack or in your hand). Click the animal, within 10 tiles, and then click the ground where it should go, also within 10 tiles of you. If your skill check passes, the animal walks to the spot. If it fails you are told you cannot persuade it to move. The animal walks only if the spot is between 1 and 15 tiles from it when it sets off.
Only wild animals that can be tamed can be herded. A tamed animal looks tame already and will not move for the crook.
# How hard it is

Each animal has a taming difficulty (see Animal Taming for the list), and the harder an animal is to tame, the harder it is to herd. The skill check runs from 30 below the animal's taming difficulty to 30 to 39 above it, so an animal teaches you only while your skill is inside that range. Below the bottom you cannot move it at all. When the game tells you it was not even challenging, that animal has nothing more to teach you: move on to a harder one.
# Training it

Herd animals that suit your skill and move up as you rise. The first number is where an animal starts to teach you, the second about where it stops:
Rabbits: 0 to 15
Dogs: 0 to 20
Birds: 0 to 28
Rats, cats and chickens: 0 to 34
Sheep, cows, goats and pigs: 0 to 45
Horses and boars: 0 to 64
Grizzly bears, giant spiders and snakes: 30 to 94
Bulls: 40 to 100

Sheep, cows, goats, pigs, horses, deer, bears and ordinary wolves (not dire wolves) only fight if you attack them first, so they are safe to herd. Snakes, giant spiders, scorpions, alligators, hell cats, mongbats and giant rats attack on sight, so herd those only when you can defend yourself. Make sure the arrow beside the skill in your skills window is set to Up, or it will not gain (see Skill locks 101 in [Welcome).
# What you need
A Shepherd's Crook costs about 20 gold from a blacksmith or a weaponsmith. It is also a light staff you can fight with.
# Good to know
It does not repeat on its own: you click the animal and the ground each time.
# What it is
Animal Taming makes a wild animal your pet. A pet follows you, fights for you and obeys spoken orders, and some can carry your goods or be ridden. The animals worth having ask for a lot of skill.
# Taming step by step

1. Use Animal Taming (the button beside it in your skills window), or click a wild animal once and choose Tame from its menu.
2. Click the animal. It must be within 2 tiles of you.
3. Stay within 6 tiles of it, in sight, for 9 to 12 seconds. The attempt stops if you leave, lose sight of it, die, or anyone hurts the animal.
4. The game then rolls your skill. If it works, the animal accepts you as its master and follows you. If not, you may try again at once.

You cannot try an animal whose taming difficulty (below) is higher than your skill. At its number your chance is almost nothing; it rises evenly to certain 50 points above, so 25 above gives an even chance. Each earlier owner makes the roll 6 points harder, and an animal with 5 owners cannot be tamed. An animal you owned before is yours again with no roll, and teaches you nothing.
# Which animals

Taming difficulty of most of the tameable animals in the world (one control slot unless noted):
Rabbits, gorillas, mongbats, dogs, birds, rats, cats and chickens: below 0 (no skill needed)
Sheep, cows, goats and pigs: 11.1
Eagles: 17.1
Timber wolves, deer, slimes and bullfrogs: 23.1
Horses, desert and forest ostards, rideable llamas, boars and giant rats: 29.1
Llamas, walruses, polar bears and black bears: 35.1
Brown bears and cougars: 41.1
Alligators and scorpions: 47.1
Panthers, grey wolves and snow leopards: 53.1
Grizzly bears, giant spiders, snakes and great harts: 59.1
White wolves: 65.1
Hell cats and bulls: 71.1
Dire wolves: 83.1
Drakes: 84.3 (2 slots)
Dragons: 93.9 (3 slots)
Nightmares: 95.1 (2 slots)
White wyrms: 96.3 (3 slots)

Sheep, cows, pigs, goats, horses, deer, bears, big cats and ordinary wolves only fight if you attack them first, so taming them is safe. Snakes, giant spiders, scorpions, alligators, hell cats, mongbats, giant rats, sewer rats and dire wolves attack on sight. Dragons, white wyrms and nightmares usually just get angry instead of being tamed (19 times in 20) and attack you.
# Your pets

Your pets together may use 5 control slots. Most animals use 1; a drake or nightmare uses 2, and a dragon or white wyrm 3. A pet that would take you over 5 is refused: you are told you have too many followers.

Give orders by speaking within 14 tiles of your pets, or click a pet once for a menu of the same orders. Start with all for every pet, or use a pet's name:
all follow me, all stay, all stop, all come, all guard me
all kill or all attack (then click the target), all follow (then click who to follow)
With a name you can also say friend, drop, release or transfer.

A pet listed at 29.1 or lower always obeys. A harder pet obeys only some of the time. Your Taming counts four times and your Animal Lore once, set against the pet's number: when that mix equals the number the pet obeys 7 times in 10, and 5 points above it nearly always. Below the number it loses 14 percent for every point short (never under 22 percent), and each point of loyalty it is missing takes off 1 percent more.

Loyalty is how much a pet likes you, out of 100. Every hour that a pet stands in the world it loses 10, even while you are logged out, and at 0 it decides it is better off without you and goes wild. To raise it, drag food it likes onto it (Animal Lore shows what it eats): each piece has an even chance of adding 10. A pet in a stable, or a mount you are riding, loses none.
# Stables and release

Say stable to an animal trainer and click the pet to leave there. It costs 30 gold, from your pack or bank, and a pack animal must be unloaded first. Say claim to get your pets back, which is free. You can keep 2 pets stabled in all, 3 when your Animal Taming, Animal Lore and Veterinary add up to 160, 4 at 200 and 5 at 240, and one more for each of the three that is 100.
To let a pet go, say its name and release, and confirm in the window. It goes wild, and it remembers you as an owner.

paragraphs.text: Taming keeps trying the same animal after each plain failure until it accepts you or something stops it. Each attempt is still the usual 9 to 12 seconds. Walking, casting, using another skill, entering war mode, fighting or being hurt end it, and so does opening any target cursor.

paragraphs: # Training it

Work up the list above as your skill rises. You can already tame the easiest animals at Animal Taming 0, and they become certain at about 30. After that, aim at animals whose number is 10 to 25 below your skill: you tame them from one try in five to one in two, and each try still teaches. A harder animal teaches more on each try, but you fail more.

An attempt takes 9 to 12 seconds, win or lose, so the skill is slow. To keep going you need a free slot: release or stable the animals you tame, but never tame the same animal twice, because it teaches nothing the second time. A trainer saves time at the start: the animal trainer in Britain teaches Animal Taming up to about 30, for 1 gold per 0.1 point (see Training in [Welcome). Make sure the arrow beside the skill in your skills window is set to Up, or it will not gain (see Skill locks 101 in [Welcome).
# What you need
Nothing but the skill and a free slot. An animal trainer also sells tame animals: a horse for about 550 gold and a pack horse for about 630.
# Good to know
There is no bonding on this shard. A pet that dies stays dead and cannot be brought back, so keep it healthy (see Veterinary) and out of fights it cannot win.

paragraphs.text: Tamed pets never attack players. A pet cannot enter or stay in a dungeon: it will not follow you through a dungeon teleporter or gate, and one tamed or dismounted inside is shrunk into your pack (double-click it outside a dungeon, with a free slot, to bring it out). You can ride one mount in and dismount it there: it stays and fights monsters. You cannot set a pet free inside a dungeon. Spell summons, familiars, hirelings, pack llamas and pack horses are not affected.

paragraphs: # What it is

Animal Lore tells you what a creature is made of: its health and stamina, its strengths, its fighting skills and what it likes to eat. It also helps the other pet skills: with Animal Taming it decides how well your pets obey, and with Veterinary it decides how much a bandage heals a pet.
# How to use it

Press the button beside Animal Lore in your skills window and click a creature within 8 tiles. You can use it again 1 second later. The skill is checked each time: your chance is about your Animal Lore divided by 120, and when it fails you are told you cannot think of anything you know offhand. When it works, a window opens with three pages; turn them with the arrows at the bottom.

At first you can look only at tamed creatures, yours or anyone's. Animal Lore 100 lets you look at wild creatures that can be tamed. Wild creatures that cannot be tamed need Animal Lore 110, and a skill stops at 100 here. You cannot use it while you are dead.
# What the window shows

Page 1: hit points, stamina and mana (current and full), Strength, Dexterity, Intelligence and armor rating.
Page 2: its Wrestling, Tactics, Magic Resistance, Anatomy and Poisoning, and its Magery, Evaluating Intelligence and Meditation. A dash means the skill is under 10.
Page 3: what food it likes, its pack instinct (the kind of pack it runs with, such as canine or feline) and how happy it is.
It does not show how hard a creature is to tame or how many control slots it uses. For that, see the list in Animal Taming.
# Why it matters

Your Animal Lore counts for 1 part in 5 of how well a harder pet obeys, with your Taming making up the rest. It also adds to the number of pets you can keep in a stable (Taming, Animal Lore and Veterinary together set it). When you bandage a pet, Animal Lore does the work Anatomy does for people: it sets how much the bandage heals, and a pet's poison can be cured only with Animal Lore 60 or more.
# Training it

Use it on a tamed creature, your own pet being the easy choice. The check runs from 0 to 120, so you can still learn at Animal Lore 100. It also trains by itself while you do pet work: every few seconds of a taming attempt on an animal you have not owned before checks it, and so does bandaging a hurt pet. So a tamer's Animal Lore rises on its own. A trainer saves time at the start: the animal trainer in Britain teaches Animal Lore up to about 21 to 33, for 1 gold per 0.1 point (see Training in [Welcome). Make sure the arrow beside the skill in your skills window is set to Up, or it will not gain (see Skill locks 101 in [Welcome).
# What you need
Nothing: Animal Lore needs no tool. You need a creature that is in sight and tamed.
# Good to know
Once you reach Animal Lore 100, use it on a wild animal that can be tamed before you tangle with it: the window shows how much health it has and which skills it fights with.
# What it is

Veterinary heals animals with bandages, chiefly your pets. It is the pet version of Healing. It uses the same bandages, but Veterinary and Animal Lore do the work that Healing and Anatomy do for people. It does not heal people; use Healing for that.
# How to use it

Double-click Bandages and click a hurt pet. You must be next to it, and stay within 1 tile of it while you work. After 3 to 5 seconds (3 with Dexterity 100 or more, 4 from 40, 5 below that) the bandage is applied. A pet that is not hurt or poisoned cannot be healed, and costs no bandage. Every other try uses one bandage, whether or not it works.
Every hit you take while you bandage makes your fingers slip: 2 percent less chance and 4 hit points less healed.
# How well it works

Your chance of healing is your Veterinary plus 10, in percent: 10 percent at 0, 60 at 50, certain from 90. A try that fails is wasted, and you are told the bandages barely helped. A try that works heals between one fifth of your Animal Lore plus one fifth of your Veterinary plus 3, and one fifth of your Animal Lore plus half of your Veterinary plus 10 hit points, and 1 more for every 100 hit points the pet can have at most. With both skills at 50 that is 23 to 45 hit points; with both at 100, 43 to 80.
# Poison

A poisoned pet can be cured with a bandage when both your Veterinary and Animal Lore are 60 or more. A bandage on a poisoned pet tries only to cure it and does not heal. Your chance is your Veterinary minus 30, doubled, in percent: 60 percent at 60 for a Lesser poison, and certain from 80. Each level above Lesser takes 10 percent off (Regular 10, Greater 20, Deadly 30, Lethal 40).
# No raising the dead
A pet that dies stays dead: there is no bonding on this shard, so there is no pet to raise. Heal your pets before they are in danger.
# Training it

Bandage a hurt pet. Each time you finish, both Veterinary and Animal Lore are checked, up to 120, whether the bandage worked or not. At very low skill most tries fail, so a trainer helps at the start: the animal trainer in Britain teaches Veterinary up to about 22 to 29, for 1 gold per 0.1 point (see Training in [Welcome). After that, let your pet fight easy monsters and bandage it afterwards. A poisoned pet trains you only when both Veterinary and Animal Lore are 60 or more. Make sure the arrow beside the skill in your skills window is set to Up, or it will not gain (see Skill locks 101 in [Welcome).
# What you need
Bandages cost about 5 gold each from a healer. A bandage weighs a tenth of a stone, so carry a stack.
# Good to know
Your pet must be next to you for the whole bandage, so heal it before it is dying and keep it near.
# What it is

Item Identification finds out what a magical weapon or armor really is. Monsters sometimes drop weapons and armor with a hidden enchantment: a weapon may be more durable, more accurate or hit harder, and armor may last longer or protect more. Until someone identifies it, such a piece is shown only as 'an unidentified long sword' or the like: you can tell that it is magical, but not what it does. Identifying it names the enchantment, and the item stays identified for good.
# How to use it

Open your skills window and click the small button beside Item Identification, then click the weapon or armor. The item can be in your pack or worn, lie on the ground in sight within 8 tiles, or be on sale in a player vendor's shop. You can use the skill again one second after the last try.

Your chance to succeed is your skill in percent: one try in two at 50.0, certain at 100.0. On success the item's full name shows over it, as if you had clicked it, and now carries the enchantment in words. Durability: durable, substantial, massive, fortified, indestructible. Accuracy: accurate, surpassingly accurate, eminently accurate, exceedingly accurate, supremely accurate. Damage: 'of ruin', 'of might', 'of force', 'of power', 'of vanquishing'. Armor protection: 'of defense', 'of guarding', 'of hardening', 'of fortification', 'of invulnerability'. Each list runs from weakest to strongest. A weapon can also be a slayer of one kind of creature, and its name says which.
If you fail, the item stays 'unidentified' and you are told 'You are not certain...'. Failing costs nothing: try again.

Anything that is not a weapon or armor only shows its name (and you are told 'You are not certain...' as well); no skill check is made, so you learn nothing. On a creature or a person it just shows the name, as a single click would.
# Training it

Only weapons and armor can teach you; every other target makes no skill check. Any piece will do, magical or plain, worn or in your pack, even one you have already identified, and the chance is the same. So there is nothing to buy: use your own gear. Every try can teach you, whether it works or not, and there is always something left to learn below 100.0, so one weapon takes you from 0 to the top. One try a second is the fastest you can go.
Jewelers in Britain also teach it for gold: a lesson takes you to about 21.0 to 33.0, at 1 gold for each 0.1 point (see Training in the Welcome guide, [Welcome).
# What you need
Nothing: no tool and no reagent, only a weapon or armor to look at. Magical ones drop from monsters.
# Good to know
An unidentified piece works exactly like an identified one; identifying only tells you what it is. Click an identified item at any time to read its name again.
Item Identification shows magic and nothing else. How worn a piece is, and how hard it hits or how well it protects, is the job of Arms Lore (see its page).
# What it is

Arms Lore tells you, in words, how worn a weapon or armor is and how good it is: how hard the weapon hits, how well the armor protects. It does not show magic (that is Item Identification) and it gives you no bonus in a fight; it only lets you read your gear.
# How to use it

Open your skills window and click the small button beside Arms Lore, then click a weapon or armor. It must be within 2 tiles of you: in your pack or worn is fine, and so is a piece on sale in a player vendor's shop. Your chance to read it is your skill in percent. If you fail you are told 'You are not certain...' and can try again a second later. Anything that is not a weapon or armor gets 'This is neither weapon nor armor.'
# What it tells you

Condition comes first, in ten steps by how much of its durability is left: 'about to fall apart' (under 10 percent), 'rather flimsy', 'somewhat badly damaged', 'rather battered', 'well-used', 'some wear and tear', 'fairly good condition', 'fairly new', 'almost new' and 'unused' (90 percent or more).

A weapon then says how hard it hits and how it strikes: stabbed, slashed, bashed, shot at long range, or just hit, and, except for bows and crossbows, whether it takes one hand or two. The damage word comes from the middle of its damage range: under 3 'scratch slightly'; 3 to 5 'minimal damage'; 6 to 10 'some damage'; 11 to 15 'hurt a fair amount'; 16 to 20 'quite a lot of damage and pain'; 21 to 25 'a superior weapon'; 26 or more 'extraordinarily deadly'. A dagger (3 to 15) reads 'some damage', a long sword (5 to 33) 'quite a lot', a bow (9 to 41) 'superior' and a halberd (5 to 49) 'extraordinarily deadly'. A weapon with poison on it also says 'It appears to have poison smeared on it.'

Armor says how well it protects, from its armor rating: 0 'no defense', up to 5 'almost no protection', up to 10 'very little protection', up to 15 'some protection against blows', up to 20 'sturdy protection', up to 25 'a superior defense', up to 30 'excellent protection', and above 30 'superbly crafted to provide maximum protection'. New body armor rates 13 for leather, 16 for studded leather, 22 for ringmail, 28 for chainmail and 40 for plate. Magic and exceptional quality add to the rating, and wear takes away from it: armor with no durability left counts for only half.
# Training it

Only weapons and armor can teach you. Any piece will do, new or worn, magical or plain, and the chance is the same, so use your own gear and buy nothing. Every try can teach you, whether it works or not, and there is always something left to learn below 100.0. One try a second is the fastest you can go.
Armorers and weaponsmiths teach it for gold: a lesson takes you to about 21.0 to 33.0, at 1 gold for each 0.1 point (see Training in the Welcome guide, [Welcome).
# What you need
Nothing but a weapon or armor to look at.
# Good to know

It reads the piece as it is now, so look at your gear after a hard fight: a weapon or armor that is 'about to fall apart' needs repair soon (the Blacksmith menu has a Repair choice; see the Blacksmithy page).
Arms Lore does not make you hit harder or take less damage, and it cannot tell a magical piece from a plain one: use Item Identification for that.
# What it is

Taste Identification tells you whether a piece of food has been poisoned. Poisoned food poisons whoever eats it, so a careful traveler tastes food from a stranger first. The answer 'nothing unusual' is always true; only a failed try leaves you unsure.
# How to use it

Open your skills window and click the small button beside Taste Identification, then click a piece of food. It must be within 2 tiles of you: in your pack is fine, and so is food on sale in a player vendor's shop. Your chance is your skill in percent: one try in two at 50.0, certain at 100.0.

You are told one of three things. 'It appears to have poison smeared on it.' means the food is poisoned. 'You detect nothing unusual about this substance.' means it is safe. 'You cannot discern anything about this substance.' means the try failed and you know nothing yet: try again. Tasting does not use the food up, and you can taste again a second later.

Food means bread, fruit, pies, cooked meat and the like. Aimed at a potion or a potion keg the skill only tells you what it is, which you can already read from its name, and it teaches nothing. Aimed at a person it says that would be inappropriate. Drinks in pitchers and bottles, and anything else that is not food, answer that you cannot taste it.
Poison on food does its work when someone eats it: the eater is poisoned. A taste first costs nothing, so taste any food that came from someone you do not trust.
# Training it

Only food can teach you; a potion or a keg makes no skill check. The cheapest practice is one piece of cheap food that you taste again and again, because it is never used up: an apple from a provisioner or a muffin from a baker or a cook costs about 3 gold. Every try can teach you, whether it works or not, and there is always something left to learn below 100.0.
Alchemists, cooks and herbalists teach it for gold: a lesson takes you to about 22.0 to 33.0, at 1 gold for each 0.1 point (see Training in the Welcome guide, [Welcome).
# What you need
Nothing but food. Provisioners, bakers, cooks, innkeepers and tavern keepers sell it; bread is about 6 gold, apples and muffins about 3.
# Good to know

Food becomes poisoned when someone uses the Poisoning skill on it. The taste does not say how strong the poison is. If you are poisoned, a Cure potion or the Cure spell can cure it; see the Cure potions help and the Poisoning page.
Taste food on sale in a player vendor's shop before you buy it. 'Nothing unusual' is safe; if all you get is 'You cannot discern anything', try again.
# What it is

Forensic Evaluation reads the scene of a crime. Aimed at a corpse it tells you who was fighting the dead person last and who has been through the body since. Aimed at a chest or box whose lock was picked, it names whoever picked it. It needs no tool.
# How to use it

Open your skills window and click the small button beside Forensic Evaluation; the game asks 'Select what you want to examine.' Then click the target, up to 10 tiles away. Using the skill makes you visible if you were hidden. You can use it again a second later.

On a corpse your chance is your skill in percent, with no minimum. On success you learn, for a human body, 'This person was killed by' a name: whoever was fighting the dead person most recently, or 'no one'. Then you learn either 'This body has been disturbed by' the names of everyone who took or used something from it, or 'This corpse has not been desecrated.' The body of an animal or monster gives only that second answer. The first reader is recorded; anyone after is told who read it first ('The forensicist NAME has already discovered that:') and still gets the answers. If you fail: 'You cannot determine anything useful.'

On a person or a creature you need Forensic Evaluation of 40.0 or more; your chance is your skill minus 40, out of 60. It tells you very little: 'You notice nothing unusual.' Below 40.0 you only get 'You cannot determine anything useful.'

On a chest or box whose lock someone has picked it says 'This lock was opened by' the name of the last picker, or 'You notice nothing unusual.' This needs no roll. The picker is forgotten once the box is locked again, and when the server restarts.
# Training it

Corpses are the practice target: below 40.0 a person or creature teaches you nothing. A corpse can teach you from skill 0, and you may use the skill on the same corpse over and over, as long as it lies within 10 tiles and has not rotted away. Every try can teach you, whether it works or not, and there is always something left to learn below 100.0. After a fight, use it on what you killed.
The healer in Britain teaches it for gold: a lesson takes you to about 27.0 to 33.0, at 1 gold for each 0.1 point (see Training in the Welcome guide, [Welcome).
# What you need
Nothing: no tool and no reagent, only a corpse, or a lock someone picked.
# Good to know

Anyone can loot a player's body on this shard (see Dying in the Welcome guide), so the list of names on a body is how you learn who has been through your things. It does not say what was taken, and it shows no murder counts or reasons.
The 'killed by' name is whoever was fighting the victim most recently, which is usually, but not always, who struck the last blow.
# What it is

Musicianship is the skill of playing an instrument well. Every note you play is checked against it: with Musicianship at 50.0 your music goes wrong half the time, and at 100.0 it never does. The three bard skills (Peacemaking, Provocation and Discordance) all begin with that check, so Musicianship comes first for any bard. By itself it does nothing but train.
# How to use it

You cannot use Musicianship from the skills window ('That skill cannot be used directly'). Double-click an instrument in your pack instead: it plays, with a good sound or a poor one. After each double-click you must wait 6 seconds ('You must wait to perform another action'). The instrument you play last is remembered as the one your bard skills use, for as long as it stays in your pack. Playing by double-click does not use the instrument up.
# Training it

This is the cheapest skill a bard has: double-click an instrument every 6 seconds. It costs nothing. Every play can teach you, good or poor, and its roll is your skill out of 120, so it keeps teaching all the way to 100.0.

Raise it first, to 50.0 or more, before you work on the other bard skills: a poor note wastes the whole try and a charge of the instrument, so with Musicianship at 50.0 half of those tries are lost, and at 0 none get through. The bard skills train it too, because each try rolls Musicianship, but at the price of a charge each time.
Bards teach it for gold: a lesson takes you to about 21.0 to 33.0, at 1 gold for each 0.1 point (see Training in the Welcome guide, [Welcome).
# What you need

An instrument. The bard in Lord British's Conservatory of Music in Britain sells drums, tambourines, lap harps and lutes for about 21 gold each, and the carpenter in The Saw Horse sells the same four at the same price. A tambourine weighs 1 stone, drums 4, a lute 5 and a lap harp 10; the big harp, at 35, is not sold.

A new instrument has 350 to 450 uses. Playing it by double-click uses none; every try of Peacemaking, Provocation or Discordance that gets as far as the music uses one, whether it works or not. When the last use goes you are told 'The instrument played its last tune.' and it is gone, so carry a spare. An exceptional instrument has more uses, and lowers a creature's difficulty by 5 for your bard skills.

A new character who starts with Musicianship, Peacemaking, Provocation or Discordance begins with an instrument for each, picked at random from drums, harp, lap harp, lute and tambourine. They are newbied, so they stay with you when you die (a murderer loses them). The Bard template starts with Musicianship 50.0 and Provocation 50.0.
A carpenter can also make an instrument from logs and cloth, but it needs Musicianship 45.0 as well as Carpentry from about 58 (drums, tambourine) to 79 (harp). Most players simply buy one.
# Good to know

The 6 seconds between plays apply to double-clicking only; each bard skill has its own wait. If an instrument leaves your pack while a bard skill waits for your target, you are told 'The instrument you are trying to play is no longer in your backpack!'
The harp you may start with is the heavy one, 35 stones. If it slows you, leave it in your bank and buy a lute, which weighs 5.
# What it is

Peacemaking stops fights with music. Played at one creature it calms that creature for a while: it stops fighting and stays that way until the calm runs out. Played at yourself it ends every fight within earshot, but only for a moment. It needs an instrument, and your Musicianship is checked first.
# How to use it

Open your skills window and click the small button beside Peacemaking. If you have no instrument chosen you are asked 'What instrument shall you play?': click one in your pack. After that, the last instrument you played or chose is used for as long as it stays in your pack. Then click the creature to calm, or click yourself to calm everyone around. The instrument must be in your pack when you click.
The song reaches 8 tiles, plus 1 for every 15 points of Peacemaking: 8 at 0, 10 at 30, 12 at 60, 14 at 90.

Every try starts with a Musicianship check. Your chance of playing well is your Musicianship in percent. A poor note wastes the try and one charge of the instrument ('You play poorly, and there is no effect.'), and at Musicianship 0 you never get past it.
# Calming one creature

You can calm a creature you could attack. Shopkeepers, familiars and some monsters cannot be calmed ('You have no chance of calming that creature.'), and one that is already calm refuses a second song.

How hard it is depends on the creature's difficulty. That number grows with the creature's hit points, stamina, mana and skills. It is higher for spellcasters, fire breathers and creatures that cannot be poisoned, and for creatures whose attack poisons. The game does not show it, but a weak animal is far below a strong monster, and two creatures of one kind differ a little because each rolls its own strength.

You need Peacemaking of at least the difficulty minus 35 to have any chance. Your chance then rises evenly to half at the difficulty minus 10 and certain at the difficulty plus 15. On success the creature stops fighting for 100 seconds minus two thirds of (the difficulty minus 10), never less than 10 or more than 120, so a weak creature stays calm longer than a strong one. Hurting it can wake it early, with a chance that grows the more hurt it is (about 1 in 1,000 per hit point it has lost, each time it is hit). When the calm ends it fights again. The wait before your next skill is 5 seconds after a success and 10 after a failure.
# Calming everyone

Click yourself. Your chance is your Musicianship in percent times your Peacemaking out of 120: about one try in five with both at 50.0, five in six with both at 100.0. On success every creature in reach that you could attack, and that can be calmed, drops its target and stops fighting ('You play your hypnotic music, stopping the battle.'). The calm lasts one second, so anything still angry can start again at once; it is a pause, not a peace. If nothing is in reach you are told so. The wait is 5 seconds after a success, 10 after a failure.

paragraphs.text: Other players are affected only when you could lawfully attack them (see Fighting other players in the Welcome guide, [Welcome). For anyone else the song does nothing, and a single player target answers 'You cannot calm that!'

paragraphs: # Training it

The surest way is to calm yourself. It needs no creature, you can do it safely in town, and its roll is your Peacemaking out of 120, so it keeps teaching all the way to 100.0. It costs one instrument charge a try. Only a try with good music reaches the Peacemaking roll, so raise Musicianship first (it is free; see its page): with Musicianship at 50.0 half of your charges are wasted.

Calming creatures teaches you too, but only while your skill is inside the creature's range, from its difficulty minus 35 up to its difficulty plus 15. A creature that is too weak for you teaches you nothing, and so does one that is too tough: move on to stronger creatures as your skill rises, and when you can no longer find one in that range, calm yourself instead.
A bard teaches it for gold: a lesson takes you to about 22.0 to 29.0 (the guildmaster 27.0 to 33.0), at 1 gold for each 0.1 point (see Training in the Welcome guide, [Welcome).
# What you need

An instrument. The bard in Lord British's Conservatory of Music and the carpenter in The Saw Horse, both in Britain, sell drums, tambourines, lap harps and lutes for about 21 gold each. Each new one has 350 to 450 uses and every try uses one: see the Musicianship page.
# Good to know

Using any bard skill makes you visible if you were hidden. While the cursor waits for your target you cannot use another skill, and a skill used too soon answers 'You must wait a few moments to use another skill.'
A calm creature is not tamed or friendly: when the calm ends it is as hostile as before. Use the time to kill it, or to leave.
# What it is

Provocation turns two creatures on each other. You play for one creature, it becomes angry, and you then pick a second creature for it to attack. The two fight each other instead of you. A bard uses it to thin out a pack, or to win a fight without drawing a sword.
# How to use it

Open your skills window and click the small button beside Provocation. If you have no instrument chosen you are asked to click one in your pack; after that the last one you used is remembered while it stays in your pack. The game asks 'Whom do you wish to incite?': click the first creature. It answers 'You play your music and your target becomes angered. Whom do you wish them to attack?': click the second.

Both must be creatures that you could attack, and they cannot be the same one ('You can't tell someone to attack themselves!'). A tamed pet picked first answers 'They are too loyal to their master to be provoked.' An innocent (blue) creature picked first, such as a townsperson or a shopkeeper, answers 'Think not that I fail to see what thou art doing!' and you lose 75 karma. If either creature cannot be provoked (shopkeepers, familiars and some monsters), your second click answers 'You have no chance of provoking those creatures.' Each click can reach 8 tiles, plus 1 for every 15 points of Provocation, and the two creatures must be that close to each other.

Your Musicianship is checked first. Your chance of playing well is your Musicianship in percent; a poor note wastes the try and one charge of the instrument ('You play poorly, and there is no effect.').
# Results by skill

How hard it is depends on the creatures' difficulty. That number grows with a creature's hit points, stamina, mana and skills. It is higher for spellcasters, fire breathers and creatures that cannot be poisoned, and for creatures whose attack poisons. The game does not show it, but a weak animal is far below a strong monster, and two creatures of one kind differ a little because each rolls its own strength.

Take the average difficulty of the two creatures. You need Provocation of at least that average minus 30 to have any chance. The chance then rises evenly to half at the average minus 5 and certain at the average plus 20. On success: 'Your music succeeds, as you start a fight.' On failure: 'Your music fails to incite enough anger.' You wait 10 seconds before the next skill after a success and 5 after a failure.

The two fight until one of them dies, or until they are more than about 16 tiles apart (most creatures notice that far). After the first 30 seconds a creature also stops if you are more than that far from it. The one that wins goes back to its normal behavior and may turn on you, so provoke from a distance and be ready.
# Training it

Use pairs of creatures, and keep to a pair whose average difficulty is between your skill minus 20 and your skill plus 30, because a try teaches only while your skill is inside the window: a pair that is too weak for you teaches you nothing, and a pair that is too tough gives you no chance. Start with weak creatures and move on to stronger pairs as your skill rises; near the top only the strongest monsters are hard enough, so expect to finish in a dungeon with care.

Raise Musicianship first (it is free; see its page): with it at 50.0, half of your tries and charges are wasted. If you start as a Bard you begin with Provocation and Musicianship both at 50.0, so you can already try fairly strong pairs.
A bard teaches it for gold: a lesson takes you to about 20.0 to 28.0 (the guildmaster 27.0 to 33.0), at 1 gold for each 0.1 point (see Training in the Welcome guide, [Welcome).
# What you need

An instrument. The bard in Lord British's Conservatory of Music and the carpenter in The Saw Horse, both in Britain, sell drums, tambourines, lap harps and lutes for about 21 gold each. Each new one has 350 to 450 uses and every try that reaches the second creature uses one: see the Musicianship page.
# Good to know
Using any bard skill makes you visible if you were hidden. If you try again too soon you are told 'You must wait a few moments to use another skill.'
# What it is

Discordance is a bard's song that weakens a creature. While it plays on, the creature loses part of its Strength, Dexterity and Intelligence (so also its hit points, stamina and mana) and the same share of every skill it has. The share is your Discordance divided by 5, in percent, rounded down: 5 percent at 25.0, 10 at 50.0, 20 at 100.0. It works on creatures only, never on players.
# How to use it

Open your skills window and click the small button beside Discordance. If you have no instrument chosen you are asked to click one in your pack; after that the last one you used is remembered while it stays in your pack. The game asks you to 'Choose the target for your song of discordance.': click a creature. The song reaches 8 tiles, plus 1 for every 15 points of Discordance.

Your Musicianship is checked first. Your chance of playing well is your Musicianship in percent; a poor note wastes the try and one charge of the instrument ('You play poorly, and there is no effect.').

You cannot sing discord at yourself, at a shopkeeper, a familiar or a monster that is immune, or at a creature you could not attack: 'A song of discord would have no effect on that.' Aimed at a player it does nothing at all: the instrument just sounds badly, and nothing is used up. A creature can carry only one song at a time ('That creature is already in discord.').
# Results by skill

How hard it is depends on the creature's difficulty. That number grows with the creature's hit points, stamina, mana and skills. It is higher for spellcasters, fire breathers and creatures that cannot be poisoned, and for creatures whose attack poisons. The game does not show it, but a weak animal is far below a strong monster, and two creatures of one kind differ a little because each rolls its own strength.

You need Discordance of at least the difficulty minus 35 to have any chance. Your chance then rises evenly to half at the difficulty minus 10 and certain at the difficulty plus 15. On success: 'You play jarring music, suppressing your target's strength.' On failure: 'You attempt to disrupt your target, but fail.' You wait 12 seconds before your next skill after any try on a creature.

The song lasts as long as you stay alive, visible and within reach of the creature. If you die, hide or move out of reach, it ends 15 seconds later (come back in time and it carries on). It also ends when the creature dies.
# Training it

It needs a creature, so it trains slowly: one try every 12 seconds at best, and a creature that is already in discord cannot be sung at again until the song ends. Use it on the creatures you are fighting anyway, and choose ones that are tough enough: a try teaches only while your skill is inside the window, from the difficulty minus 35 up to the difficulty plus 15. A creature that is too weak for you teaches you nothing, and so does one that is too tough, so move on to stronger creatures as your skill rises.
Raise Musicianship first (it is free; see its page): with it at 50.0, half of your tries and charges are wasted.
A bard teaches it for gold: a lesson takes you to about 21.0 to 33.0, at 1 gold for each 0.1 point (see Training in the Welcome guide, [Welcome).
# What you need

An instrument. The bard in Lord British's Conservatory of Music and the carpenter in The Saw Horse, both in Britain, sell drums, tambourines, lap harps and lutes for about 21 gold each. Each new one has 350 to 450 uses and every try on a creature uses one: see the Musicianship page.
# Good to know

Using any bard skill makes you visible if you were hidden, and if you hide again, a song you already sing ends 15 seconds later. The song lowers stats and skills only; it takes nothing else from the creature, and it does not stop it fighting. Sing before the hard part of a fight, then stay within reach.
# What it is
Hiding makes you unseen. While you stay hidden, other players and monsters cannot see you unless they find you. Stealth builds on it. It is also a quiet way to wait out of sight.
# How to use it

Click the button beside Hiding in your skills window. If it works you are told "You have hidden yourself well." and war mode is switched off. If it fails you are told "You fail to hide." Either way no skill can be used again for 10 seconds.

You cannot hide while you are casting a spell. You cannot hide with an enemy in sight either: if the creature or player you are fighting, or anyone who is fighting you, can see you from within a certain number of tiles, you are told "You can't seem to hide right now." That number is 18 tiles up to Hiding 80, then it shrinks to 8 tiles at Hiding 100. Break line of sight first (for example by going round a corner), then hide.
# Staying hidden

Anything loud or busy reveals you: speaking, swinging a weapon or firing a bow, casting a spell, drinking a potion, using a bandage, throwing an explosion potion, giving a pet an order, taking something from a corpse that is not yours, pushing past someone, using Stealing or Begging, and sometimes a failed try at Snooping. Poison reveals you about 2 times in 5 each time it hurts you.
Taking a step reveals you at once. The one exception is Stealth, which gives you silent steps (see the Stealth page; it needs Hiding 80). Running, or riding a mount, always reveals you.
# Who can find you

A player who uses Detecting Hidden finds you when their skill, give or take 10, is at least your Hiding, give or take 10. A player who is allowed to attack you also gets a free roll like that, with no skill button, whenever you or they move within 4 tiles of each other, so a hidden thief standing still can be found when the other player walks by. Party members and guild allies never find each other this way.
A monster that has the Detecting Hidden skill looks for hidden players in sight now and then, roughly every half minute to two minutes. A higher Hiding and Stealth make you harder for it to find.
# Training it

Each try succeeds with a chance equal to your Hiding out of 100: 30 in 100 at skill 30. The lower your chance, the more often a try teaches. At skill 0 you cannot succeed yet, but every try still teaches until 10.0, so just keep trying. With 10 seconds between tries you get about six a minute.

Train somewhere quiet where nothing is fighting you, such as a town street. Do not train inside a house you own or are a friend of: Hiding always works there, so it teaches nothing. Beside or inside any other house you get a bonus of 50 on the roll, which makes it easier, but then it stops teaching at skill 50.
The Rangers' Guildmaster and the Thieves' Guildmaster in Britain teach Hiding for 1 gold per 0.1 point, up to a third of their own skill: about 22 to 33 (see Training in [Welcome).
# What you need
Nothing: no tool, no reagent and no gold. You need room to be unseen, away from anyone who is fighting you.
# Good to know

Hiding turns war mode off. A failed Snooping try reveals you with a chance of 1 minus half your Hiding, so 50 in 100 at Hiding 100. Hiding is not an escape from a fight you are already in: it will not work until your enemies lose sight of you.
# What it is

Stealth lets you move while you stay hidden. Without it your first step reveals you. With it you get silent steps: one for every 10 points of Stealth, and at least one, so 10 at Stealth 100. The step after your last silent one reveals you.
# How to use it

Hide first (see the Hiding page), then click the button beside Stealth in your skills window. If you are not hidden you are told "You must hide first." You need Hiding of 80.0 or more; with less you are told "You are not hidden well enough. Become better at hiding." and you are revealed. When it works you are told "You begin to move quietly." and you may walk your silent steps. A failed roll says "You fail in your attempt to move unnoticed." and reveals you. Afterwards no skill can be used for 10 seconds.
Running, or riding a mount, always reveals you, Stealth or not. Everything else that reveals a hidden character (see Hiding) reveals a stealthy one too.

Armor counts. At an armor rating of 26 or more you are told "You could not hope to move quietly wearing this much armor." and you are revealed. Below that, armor makes the roll harder (see Training). A full set of ordinary new leather armor has an armor rating of 13.
# Training it
Stealth cannot be used, and so cannot be trained, until your Hiding is 80.0. Train Hiding first.
The Rangers' Guildmaster (about 20 to 28) and the Thieves' Guildmaster (about 28 to 33) in Britain teach Stealth for 1 gold per 0.1 point, once your Hiding is 80.0 (see Training in [Welcome).

On each try your chance is your Stealth plus 20, minus twice your armor rating, out of 100. With no armor that is 20 in 100 at Stealth 0, and certain at 80. A roll that cannot fail teaches nothing, so with no armor you stop learning at 80. Each point of armor rating moves both ends of that range up by 2. In a full set of leather armor the range is 6 to 106, so if you wear it from Stealth 80 you keep learning all the way to 100. Below Stealth 6 leather is too much: you cannot succeed and you learn nothing.

You do not have to walk to learn. Hide in a quiet place, then use Stealth. When it works you are still hidden, so you can use it again every 10 seconds, and each use is a new roll. After a failed roll you are revealed: hide again first, and remember that Hiding and Stealth each need their 10 seconds, so a fail costs you about 20.
# What you need

Nothing for the skill itself, only Hiding 80. For the last 20 points, leather armor: a tanner in Britain sells the pieces for about 405 gold in all (cap 10, gloves 60, gorget 74, arms 80, legs 80 and tunic 101).
# Good to know
Your silent steps are counted from the moment Stealth works. Using Stealth again refills them to the full count, so you do not have to wait until they run out. If you are revealed, they are lost.
Detecting Hidden used on you is rolled against your Hiding alone. A monster's search counts both your Hiding and your Stealth, so it finds you more easily if either one is low.
# What it is
Stealing takes an item out of a pack or a container, and sometimes you are noticed doing it. Stealing from another player has strict rules here, set out below.
# How to use it

Empty your hands, weapon and shield too, or you are told "Both hands must be free to steal." Stand next to your target, click the button beside Stealing in your skills window and choose it. Choose an item in an open container to take that item. Choose a person or creature and a random item from its backpack is picked for you; to pick the item yourself, open the pack first with Snooping. You can use the skill again 10 seconds after you used it.
# What you can take

The item, with everything in it, can weigh 10 stones at most, and your pack needs room for it. You cannot steal anything worn or held, anything lying on the ground or on a corpse, anything in a locked container, newbied items, blessed items, or anything from a vendor that a player runs.

Heavy things are harder. The roll uses the item's weight in stones, rounded up to a whole number, times 10: you have no chance below that number minus 22.5, and the chance rises evenly to certain at 50 points above it. The skill you need to have any chance, and to be sure:
1 stone: any skill, 37.5
3 stones: 7.5, 57.5
5 stones: 27.5, 77.5
10 stones: 77.5, never
From a stack you get a random part of the pile, no heavier than a tenth of your Stealing in stones (at least one item), and the weight of that part sets the difficulty.
# Being noticed

Being noticed is a separate roll, made whether or not you got the item: you are noticed when a number from 0 to 149 is above your Stealing. That is nearly every try at skill 0, two tries in three at 50 and one in three at 100. It matters only when the victim is a person or creature: nobody sees you take from a container nobody carries.

If you are noticed stealing from someone who was innocent to you, you become a criminal for 2 minutes, and everyone within 8 tiles is told what they saw. A criminal is chased by guards in a guarded town, refused by bankers and healers, and cannot cast Recall or Gate Travel. Being noticed stealing from someone who is already a criminal or murderer to you does not make you one.

Every try costs about 50 karma (more if your karma is high), whether it works or not. A stolen item that is not a stack or a container is marked for 2 minutes: you cannot trade it, and if you die carrying it, it goes back to the person or creature you took it from.
# Stealing from other players

You can steal from another player only if you belong to the Thieves' Guild. A guild member who has murder counts is suspended and cannot. Guards also take no murder report against a Thieves' Guild member.

To join, find the Thieves' Guildmaster in the warehouse on Bay Side Road, in the south-east of Britain (click the guildmaster to read the name), say the name and "join", and give 500 gold. You need a character at least 7 days old that has played at least 2 days, is not Young, has no murder counts and has trained Stealing to at least 60.0.

paragraphs.text: You also need a victim you are allowed to attack: a player who has Criminal Intent on, a criminal, a murderer, someone already fighting you, or someone at guild war with you. A player who has not turned Intent on (see [Intent) cannot be robbed: the try is refused.

In a Hot Zone (Fire Island, Buccaneer's Den island and Hythloth) players can attack one another freely, and the same goes for stealing between two players who are both in the same Hot Zone. A Backpack Ward does nothing there.

Banks are off limits. If you or your victim stand in the square of 24 by 24 tiles around one of 17 town banks, you cannot steal from a player: "You cannot steal from players in this bank protection area." A Backpack Ward cannot be stolen either, nor can anything bound to its owner: "That protected item cannot be stolen."

Many players carry a Backpack Ward, which watches for thieves (see the Backpack Ward page of the Welcome guide, [Welcome). It does not change your chance to steal. But after a theft from its carrier that nobody noticed, the Ward rolls on its own to expose you: 25 in 100 after your first such theft from that player, 50 in 100 after the second, certain after the third. If it exposes you, you become a criminal, are told "You have been caught stealing!", and cannot steal from that player again, with any of your characters, while the Ward lasts: about 30 quiet minutes.
A Knocked Out player cannot be robbed with Stealing. The Snooping page explains how a Knocked Out player's pack can be opened instead.

paragraphs: # Training it

A roll teaches only while your skill is between an item's two numbers in the list above (the skill that gives you any chance and the skill that makes it certain): below the first you cannot succeed and learn nothing, above the second you always succeed and learn nothing. Inside that window a roll teaches whether you get the item or not, and below 10.0 every one does. After that you learn most from things a little too heavy for you: choose items that weigh about one stone more than a tenth of your skill (1 stone at skill 0, 3 at skill 20, 6 at 50, 9 at 80), which gives roughly a 1 in 4 chance. Even a 10-stone item gives only 45 in 100 at skill 100.
The Thieves' Guildmaster in Britain teaches Stealing for 1 gold per 0.1 point, up to a third of its own skill: about 30 to 33, whether or not you belong to the guild (see Training in [Welcome).

The only tries that cannot get you noticed are items in a container that nobody carries, such as a chest or crate. If it is locked, pick the lock first. Every try still costs karma. Do not practise on shopkeepers or townspeople: a noticed thief is a criminal, and in a guarded town the guards come.
# What you need
Nothing to buy: empty hands and a little room in your pack.
# Good to know
Stealing reveals you if you were hidden. It never gives murder counts; only killing does. Buccaneer's Den has no guards.

paragraphs.text: While you are a criminal, any player may attack you.
Being Knocked Out does not save a criminal: a criminal who is brought down by another player dies.

paragraphs: # What it is
Snooping lets you open and look inside a pack or container that someone else carries, without being asked. You only look. To take something you need the Stealing skill.
# How to use it

Snooping has no skill button. Stand next to the owner and double-click the backpack on their paperdoll (double-click them to open it), or a bag or box they carry. You must be within 1 tile of it, or you are told "That is too far away." Your chance is your Snooping out of 100. If it works the container opens for you; if not you are told "You failed to peek into the container." A locked box will not open: you are told it appears to be locked. A trapped box sets off its trap on you instead of opening.
# Being noticed

Before your roll, the game checks whether anyone notices you. With a chance of 100 minus your skill, out of 100, everyone within 8 tiles, the owner too, is told that you were seen attempting to peek into the owner's belongings. That happens whether your peek works or not, and never at Snooping 100.

Snooping is not a crime: it does not make you a criminal. It costs about 4 karma a try, though. If you are hidden and a try fails, you are revealed with a chance of 1 minus half your Hiding (50 in 100 at Hiding 100).
# Who you can snoop
Any non-player who is not staff, shopkeepers and townspeople included. A player only if you are allowed to attack them; otherwise you are told "You cannot perform negative acts on your target."

paragraphs.text: That is the Safe World rule: a player who has Criminal Intent on, a criminal, a murderer, someone already fighting you, or someone at guild war with you. A player who has not turned Intent on (see [Intent) cannot be snooped.
In a Hot Zone (Fire Island, Buccaneer's Den island and Hythloth), players who are both in the same Hot Zone can snoop one another.

A Knocked Out player cannot be snooped with the skill. In a Hot Zone anyone may open a Knocked Out player's pack with no roll, no karma loss and no notice, and a player who was not already a criminal becomes one on taking an item. Elsewhere only a criminal or murderer who knocked the player out may.

paragraphs: # Training it

The safe way to train is on non-players: stand beside a shopkeeper or townsperson and double-click their backpack, again and again. There is no skill wait between tries and no guard reacts. The costs are about 4 karma a try and, at low skill, almost always a notice to anyone nearby.
Your chance is your skill out of 100. Each try below 10.0 still teaches. Past that, the lower your chance, the more often a try teaches.
The Thieves' Guildmaster in Britain teaches Snooping for 1 gold per 0.1 point, up to a third of its own skill: about 30 to 33 (see Training in [Welcome).
# What you need
Nothing to buy. Hiding helps a little, because a hidden snooper is revealed less often after a failed try.
# Good to know

Snooping only looks. To take an item from a pack you have opened you need Stealing too (see that page; from another player it also takes the Thieves' Guild). Snooping a staff member is always refused.
# What it is
Lockpicking opens a locked chest, box or crate without its key. You use it through lockpicks, not a skill button. It cannot open doors, and it cannot open a lock made by magic.
# How to use it

Double-click a lockpick in your pack and choose a locked container within 1 tile. After 3 seconds you get one roll. On success you are told "The lock quickly yields to your skill." and the container is unlocked. On failure you are told "You are unable to pick the lock." and 1 failed try in 4 breaks the lockpick. If you move out of reach during the 3 seconds, the try is lost.

paragraphs.text: After a failed try the same lock is tried again for you while you have picks left and it is still locked. Walking, casting, using another skill, war mode, fighting or being hurt, or opening another target cursor stops it.

paragraphs: # Locks

Every lock has a required skill and a range. Below the required skill you are told "You don't see how that lock can be manipulated." and no pick is lost, so testing a lock costs you only 3 seconds. From the required skill you may try; your chance rises evenly across the range, from nothing at its low number to certain at its top. A lock that cannot be picked says "This lock cannot be picked by normal means..." A container that is not locked says "This does not appear to be locked."

A chest that refills itself after you take things out of it comes in three strengths, as range and required skill: the weakest from -10 to 30, needing 0; the middle from 20 to 60, needing 30; the strongest ordinary ones from 50 to 90, needing 60. After you take things out it refills, locks again and may get a new trap, within 60 to 90 minutes. A chest from a treasure map is harder: its required skill is 36, 76, 84, 92 or 100 for levels 1 to 5, and its range runs from 10 below that to 40 above.

You can make a lock yourself. A box or crate made with Carpentry comes with a key inside, and with a lock, if the maker's Tinkering roll works (it always does from Tinkering 15). Lock it with the key (double-click the key, then point at the box) and pick it as often as you like. The lock gets stronger with the maker's Tinkering: at 50 it needs 36 and teaches 26 to 75, and from a maker at 100 it needs 76 and teaches 66 to 95.
# Training it

Your chance is how far your skill lies between the lock's low and high numbers. A roll can teach you, whether it works or not, as long as your skill is inside the lock's range, and a lock that is hard for you teaches more often. While your skill is below 10.0 every roll teaches. So aim for locks a little above you.

Roughly: from 0 to 30 pick the weakest locks, which you can try from the start. From 30 to 60 pick the middle ones, from 60 to 90 the strongest ordinary ones, and past 90 chests from treasure maps of level 3 or more.

A lesson from a Tinker, the Tinkers' Guildmaster or the Thieves' Guildmaster in Britain is a shortcut: it raises you to between about 20 and 33, for 1 gold for each 0.1 point (see Training in the Welcome guide, [Welcome).
# What you need

Lockpicks. They stack. Provisioners sell them for about 12 gold each (20 in stock) and buy them back for 6. A character with Tinkering can make one from a single iron ingot (Tinkering 45 to 95). Buy a handful before you start, because a failed try breaks one in four.
# Good to know

Many locked chests are trapped. The trap goes off when you open the chest after picking it (a trap set with Tinkering goes off when the lock is picked). A trap either burns you for 10 to 30 damage times the chest's level or poisons you, more strongly at a higher level. Chests that refill themselves are level 1 to 3; chests from treasure maps are level 1 to 5 and always burn. Before you open a chest, point Detecting Hidden at it: "[trapped]" shows over a trapped one when the search works. Remove Trap disarms it (see that page).
A chest sealed with the Magic Lock spell cannot be picked: it needs its key, or the Unlock spell if your Magery is strong enough for that lock.
# What it is

Remove Trap disarms the traps that guard chests, boxes and crates. A trap can burn, poison or hurt whoever opens the container or picks its lock, so a thief who opens other people's property needs this skill.
# How to use it

You need Lockpicking 50 and Detecting Hidden 50 before you can use it. With less you are told "You do not know enough about locks. Become better at picking locks." or "You are not perceptive enough.
